1032-the-pupil:
Henry James tells of Pemberton, a young tutor hired to teach Morgan Moreen, a brilliant boy of twelve, in a grand but shabby family that never pays its bills. The Moreens charm, flatter, and stall, while the boy grows wiser than his parents and fonder of his tutor. The tale is set in hotels and villas in France and Italy.

Pemberton must choose between a wage he never gets and a pupil he loves, and Morgan, ill and keen-eyed, sees the trap before he does. The novella turns on money, manners, and affection, and it ends with a quiet shock. James packs a whole moral tangle into a short, polished story.
10696-the-danger-trail:
James Oliver Curwood published The Danger Trail in 1910, a romance of the Canadian North. Howland, the hero, meets a girl of the snows, hears a mysterious attack and a midnight warning, and is drawn into a race into the North. Chapters promise a house of red death, a fight, a pursuit, and at last Jean's story and the secret of Meleese.

Curwood writes of snow, stars, and danger with the pace of a thriller and the warmth of a love story. The North itself, cold and vast, shapes every scene. Readers who enjoy early adventure fiction will find here a fast tale of love, peril, and loyalty on the frontier.
1082-voyage-of-the-paper-canoe-a-geograp:
Nathaniel H. Bishop paddled a paper canoe 2,500 miles down the American coast, from Quebec to the Gulf of Mexico, and wrote this account of the journey. A paper boat, light and tough, carried him through rivers, sounds, and swamps. Bishop, a naturalist and sportsman, chose paper for lightness on long portages.

Bishop notes geography, wildlife, and the people he met along the way, with the eye of a naturalist and a sportsman. The voyage remains a classic of American canoe travel, and a record of waterways now much changed. His 2,500-mile route, from the St. Lawrence to the Gulf, took him through waters few had mapped.
10984-growth-of-the-soil:
Knut Hamsun's Nobel Prize novel, translated from Norwegian by W. W. Worster in 1917, follows Isak, a strong settler who walks into the northern wilderness carrying a sack of food and tools. He finds a patch of ground in the common lands, builds a home, and slowly turns forest and moor into a farm. His wife Inger and their children, including Eleseus and Sivert, share the labour.

Hamsun celebrates manual work, seasons, and the land itself, while showing how money, town ways, and modern life unsettle the farm. Eleseus grows steadier through hardship, and the soil rewards patience. The novel's slow rhythm matches its theme: a life built by hand, year by year, from nothing. It remains Hamsun's best-known work in English.
11151-the-lost-trail:
Edward S. Ellis published this 1911 frontier novel, The Lost Trail, author of Seth Jones and The Forest Spy. The book opens with a verse motto from Hiawatha, then a singular occurrence in the spring of 1820 on an upper tributary of the Mississippi.

Chapters follow the shadow, adventures of a night, jug acquaintances, an ominous rencounter, gone, the lost trail, a Hibernian's search, the trail of death, the dead shot, and conclusion. The frontispiece cries, That Indian has carried Cora away, and a missionary's wife is taken from her cabin while an Indian woman hurries through the clearing. Ellis's tale of captivity, pursuit, and frontier fighting follows the dime-novel tradition he helped create.
11873-a-holiday-in-the-happy-valley-with:
Major T. R. Swinburne's 1907 Holiday in the Happy Valley, with pen and pencil, records a trip across Kashmir with twenty-four coloured illustrations. The frontispiece shows the Jhelum at Srinagar, and the book, dedicated to Jane, quotes Clough on going over great windy waters and clear-crested summits toward sea, sky, and a perfecter earth.

Swinburne writes as both soldier and sketcher, describing the valley's rivers, gardens, and mountains while his drawings fix scenes a pen alone might miss. Later contents include Udaipur, suggesting a wider Indian tour. The Happy Valley itself, its waterways and light, remains the book's center and its reason for being.
1283-tom-swift-and-his-wizard-camera-or-:
Victor Appleton sends Tom Swift around the world with a wizard camera, a motion-picture machine of his own design, to film wild beasts and strange lands for a moving-picture company. The tale moves through jungles, deserts, and storms, with the camera's crank turning through every peril.

Tom's pluck and his gadgets carry the adventure, and the book captures the wonder of early cinema. The plot is brisk and boyish, full of escapes and odd sights. It suits young readers who like Swift and the romance of the first film age.
12915-the-white-devil:
John Webster's tragedy The White Devil, published with a defiant preface to the reader, was first acted in a dull winter season before a thin, uncomprehending audience. Webster answers critics by confessing his faults freely, in Latin tags and plain English, and challenging readers to judge the play itself. The preface is famous for its proud, prickly tone.

Inside, Vittoria faces Monticelso, a cardinal turned lawyer, who paints her follies in red and white and calls her a devil who would betray a second paradise. Her spirit answers him charge for charge. The tragedy remains a dark, brilliant landmark of Jacobean drama.
12931-the-daredevil:
Maria Thompson Daviess wrote The Daredevil in 1916 as a Southern war-era romance with a bold heroine. Its heroine longs, like many women in the opening pages, for a man's doublet, hose, sword, and view of life, and the story grants her a taste of that freedom. Chapters move from sparkling waves over explosives to camps, spies, and old Harpeth timber.

A haunted-house thread adds Southern gothic flavour: a servant named Kizzie tells of a grandmother's flowered silk dress in a glass case, said to walk as a ghost in slippers and folderols. Daviess blends romance, humour, and wartime daring. The novel suits readers who like spirited heroines in old Tennessee.
13087-sammie-and-susie-littletail:
Howard R. Garis's 1910 children's book, with pictures by Louis Wisa, follows two bunny children, Sammie and Susie Littletail, through small woodland adventures. Chapters run from Sammie in a trap and his rescue to digging a burrow, helping Mrs. Wren, and a visit to the circus. Uncle Wiggily Longears, the lame old rabbit, guides them through much of it.

One day Uncle Wiggily, seized by rheumatism, cannot swim with the children and must teach from the bank. Another day Susie learns to jump rope, slow as salt, fast as pepper, and faster still as double pepper, with help from Bully the frog. The tales are gentle, funny, and made for reading aloud, with a new scrape in every chapter.
13345-vanguards-of-the-plains-a-romance-:
Margaret Hill McCarter's 1917 Vanguards of the Plains is a romance of the old Santa Fé Trail. It honors the stalwart men who defied the desert and died bravely building a highway for westward commerce. Contents run in four parts, from clearing the trail and the beginnings of a plainsman to a bull-whacker's farewell. McCarter writes with warm, patriotic feeling.

A narrator, walking a crooked street beside an old church, hears a priest's words about walls old as hate and strong as love. Later, a freighter says good-bye to Little Lees, the pressure of warm white fingers lingering as he retraces his steps to the trail's end, where Father Josef waits at the church door. The novel is a Kansas romance of trail, church, and home.
13893-compilation-of-the-messages-and-pa:
James D. Richardson compiled this volume on William McKinley, published by authority of Congress in 1902. It prints messages, proclamations, and executive orders relating to the Spanish-American War. McKinley, born in Niles, Ohio, in 1843, appears in a biographical sketch. His Scotch-Irish ancestors, Revolutionary service, and Ohio move follow.

The papers record Cuba's revolt, Spain's efforts, and the destruction war brought to the island. Richardson notes that the civilised code of war was disregarded by Spaniards and insurgents alike. The volume gives the official American record of 1898. Historians use it for McKinley's policy and rhetoric. It preserves a key presidential archive.
1417-sons-of-the-soil:
Balzac's long Burgundian novel sets peasants against their landlord at the great estate of Les Aigues. The new owner, a retired general, tries to fence his woods and stop poaching. The village folk, who have long lived off the land, answer with stealth, lawsuits, and a slow conspiracy of their own.

Through bailiffs, innkeepers, and labourers, the book shows a countryside in quiet revolt, where old custom and new property law collide. Its scale is wide and its tone stern. It remains a powerful picture of rural France torn between lord and labourer after the Revolution.
14545-copper-streak-trail:
Eugene Manlove Rhodes published this Arizona western in 1917, opening with Peter Johnson riding a shortcut through the Comobabi Range toward Silverbell and Tucson. Rhodes knew the desert country firsthand.

Johnson, Dewing, Stanley, and other riders chase a lost pocketbook, a stolen spur, and a trail of double dealing across hills and mining camps. The dialogue is laconic and funny, and the landscape of heat, dust, and distant ranges shapes every scene. The novel is a lean, atmospheric western, praised for its authentic cowboy talk. Rhodes himself had ridden the ranges he describes.
14760-report-of-the-special-committee-on:
New Zealand's 1954 report of the Special Committee on Moral Delinquency in Children and Adolescents was laid before the House of Representatives by leave. Addressed to the prime minister in September 1954, it sets out its order of reference, procedure and narrative before asking whether juvenile immorality had increased.

Chapters examine a change of pattern in sexual misbehaviour and its causes. Visual and auditory influences, school, community and home follow, with information on sex, religion and the family, changing times, law and child welfare in New Zealand. Summary conclusions and recommendations close the volume. The report is a period document, frank about anxiety and careful about evidence, and it shaped debate on youth, media and morals.
15210-darkwater-voices-from-within-the-v:
W. E. B. Du Bois's Darkwater, first published in 1920, gathers essays, stories, and poems written from within the veil of Black American life. A postscript from 1896 frames the book as thinking about selves, homes, neighbors, work, rule, women, children, beauty, death, and war. Du Bois adds a point of view: he has lived in the world but not of it.

Between sterner flights of logic, he sets small alightings of poetry, tributes to beauty amid inner torment. The book interprets the outer human drama from a veiled corner, in microcosm. Readers will find Darkwater a landmark of Black thought, lyrical, angry, and deeply humane.
15221-a-new-conscience-and-an-ancient-ev:
Jane Addams, of Hull-House in Chicago, wrote this 1912 book on prostitution and the social evil, drawing on work by the Juvenile Protective Association. She dedicates it to that group and its president, crediting field officers who gathered much of the material. Chapters trace law, wages, child protection, rescue, and social control.

Addams argues that a new conscience is rising against an ancient evil, as cities learn to shield girls and punish exploiters. Her tone is reformist, humane, and practical, rooted in settlement work. The book remains a landmark of Progressive Era social reform, frank for its day and still sobering.
15382-jess-of-the-rebel-trail:
H. A. Cody's 1921 novel Jess of the Rebel Trail, dedicated to his uncle Hiram Cody, opens with a hold-up, rebellion, and the Eb and Flo. Chapters follow Captain Samuel shopping, Eben's discovery, Martha taking a hand, and a cow's comic part. Unwelcome visitors, peril of death, and a tricky passenger raise the stakes.

Jess, a frontier heroine of pluck, moves through rebellion trails, captures, and two women's troubles toward a dream made real. Cody, author of The Frontiersman, writes in a brisk Canadian style. Adventure readers will enjoy Jess's courage, humor, and backwoods setting.
15750-pee-wee-harris-on-the-trail:
A Boy Scout story by Percy Keese Fitzhugh, author of the Tom Slade and Roy Blakeley books. Grosset and Dunlap issued it in New York with approval of the Boy Scouts of America, and pictures by H. S. Barbour. Pee-Wee Harris, the small, loud scout, takes the trail in this volume. Fitzhugh writes for boys who knew camp life firsthand.

A lone figure, a pathetic sight, and three good turns open the trail. Robbers, a message in the dark, locked doors, and a tenth case follow, before a race with death raises the stakes. A rural paradise offers rest at last. The tale praises pluck, humour, and scout loyalty, and still reads as brisk campfire fun.
16389-the-enchanted-april:
Elizabeth von Arnim's beloved novel begins on a grey February afternoon in a dull London women's club. Mrs. Wilkins, down from Hampstead to shop, spots a Times notice: a small medieval Italian castle on the Mediterranean shore, let furnished for April, with servants included. That single advertisement sets the whole story in motion.

The women who answer it trade London rain and weary marriages for wisteria, sunshine, and sea air. Over one April month, the castle works its quiet magic on each of them. The novel is gentle, funny, and warm, a tale of escape and renewal that has charmed readers for a century.
17779-the-choise-of-valentines-or-the-me:
Thomas Nash's Choice of Valentines, or the merry ballad of Nash his dildo, appears here as edited by John S. Farmer, privately printed in London in 1899 for subscribers only. Farmer's introduction notes that the poem has come down only in manuscript form. Its copies live in the Inner Temple and the Bodleian Library, and it was doubtful whether it had ever been printed before.

Farmer admits the poem has little literary merit or intrinsic value to recommend it, but holds that no document bearing on the story of human growth should be lost. Readers get a frank Elizabethan erotic poem, presented as a scholarly document. The edition suits students of Nash and of Elizabethan underground verse.
18180-tom-slade-on-mystery-trail:
Percy Keese Fitzhugh wrote this Boy Scout story, published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1921 with the approval of the Boy Scouts of America. Tom Slade and his friends are scouts at Temple Camp, and the book opens by promising a mystery solved by scouting skill and lore. Llewellyn, a first-class scout, and Orestes, winner of merit badges for architecture and music, lead the tale.

Chapters follow the three scouts, another scout, a streak of red, strange tracks, and the triumphs of Hervey and Skinny. The boys use woodcraft and watercraft to foil evil plans and do a good turn. Young readers get a camp mystery in which knots, tracks, and steady nerve matter more than luck, and a scout's duty ends in a full salute.
18556-catalogue-of-violent-and-destructi:
Rev. Miguel Saderra Maso, assistant director of the Manila Central Observatory, compiled this catalogue at Manila in 1910. It lists violent and destructive quakes in the Philippines from 1599 to 1909, with an appendix on the Marianas Islands. The work began at the request of seismologist John Milne, who sought data for a general world catalogue under the British Association.

Where Milne's list gives only date, force, and place, Saderra Maso adds towns and buildings damaged, victim counts, and other effects, using the De Rossi-Forel scale. The result is far fuller than a bare list. The catalogue remains a base source for Philippine quake history.
18988-the-first-of-april:
An anonymous author, known only as the author of The Diabolad, wrote this satiric poem in London in 1777. It is called The First of April, or The Triumphs of Folly, and it is dedicated to a celebrated duchess. The verse mocks fashion, pride, and the follies of high society on April Fools' Day.

Folly parades in shifting dress, from red to blue to green, while luxury, eunuchs, and hangers-on trail behind her in praise. The poet uses sharp, comic images to show how taste and rank chase novelty. Readers get a biting eighteenth-century satire on vanity, wealth, and the court world.
19113-the-emigrant-trail:
Geraldine Bonner wrote this 1910 novel of the overland trail to the West. It follows emigrants in five parts, from prairie to river, mountains, desert, and at last the promised land. Rain, camp life, and the slow wagon train set the opening scenes.

A young woman with a fresh, healthy face and a firm will catches the eye of David, a traveller who has seen St. Louis twice. Love, hardship, and danger grow as the train pushes west. Readers get a sweeping pioneer romance about endurance, hope, and the cost of reaching a new home.
19763-overland-red-a-romance-of-the-moon:
Overland Red is a romance of the Moonstone Canon trail in the American Southwest. Its pages recall the old mission trail worn by Padre Junípero Serra's patient feet. Replicas of mission bells now mark that dusty way at intervals. The trail once ran from the San Gabriel Valley to the shores of Monterey. Narrow then, it was already broad in promise.

Henry Herbert Knibbs wrote Westerns steeped in California and Arizona lore. Overland Red is among his best-known titles, later filmed. Trail, mission, and canon scenery carry his stories. His cowboys talk more than most pulp heroes. The romance here grows from the land itself. It is a literary Western from the genre's early shelf.
20075-frank-fairlegh-scenes-from-the-lif:
Frank Fairlegh tells, in the first person, of a boy leaving home for the first time. The subtitle calls the book Scenes from the Life of a Private Pupil. The young narrator mocks the stock way novels treat such a parting. A stock hero would sink into deep thought for the whole ride.

Fairlegh claims a more honest, funny view of school and youth. The tale follows a private pupil through scrapes, friends, and lessons. Its humor comes from the gap between book romance and real boy life. Readers get a lively Victorian school tale with a wink at its own kind.
20151-hidden-treasures-or-why-some-succe:
H. A. Lewis published Hidden Treasures in 1887, on why some succeed while others fail. Lewis laments how many young people drift with no aim in life. They forget, he says, that they owe mankind their best efforts. He recalls the parable of the servant who buried his talent.

That buried talent stands as a warning to every reader here. Success, for Lewis, grows from using one's gifts with steady will. The book offers tales and counsel meant to spur the young. Readers get a clear sample of Victorian self-help at its most earnest.
20327-the-boy-scouts-on-the-trail:
The Boy Scouts on the Trail sends French and English boys into scout adventure. Harry protests that Frank's plan will not do at all in school. Like many French boys, this one speaks English with almost no accent. To spend a week or two alone in school horrifies him.

Scout tales of the war era stress pluck, signals, and loyal teamwork. A trail, as the title promises, must be followed through risk. Boys from two nations learn trust across language and custom here. Readers get a brisk period tale of scouting spirit and boyish daring.
20887-critical-miscellanies-vol-3-of-3-e:
A strong and pure light has gone out, mourns John Morley on the death of Mr. Mill. He calls John Stuart Mill one of the greater servants of mankind. The essay stands in volume three of Morley's Critical Miscellanies as a grave tribute.

Mill's logic, liberty, and defence of women's rights fill Morley's fond survey. The two men shared a world of reform thought and letters. Morley writes as friend and judge at once, warm yet exact. Readers meet both the sage and the mourner here, in prose that shows how Victorians honoured a great mind in print.
21022-lessons-on-soil:
Village school lessons at Wye stand behind Lessons on Soil, though print shifts their shape. E. J. Russell gave them to mixed classes from the fourth to seventh standards. Harpenden's third form heard the same soil lore in its turn as well.

Russell, a leading soil chemist, teaches what soil is and how it feeds plants. Sand, clay, chalk, water, and air get plain, tested treatment for schools. His lessons link lab science to the fields outside the school door. The book shows a master of his field stooping to teach children, with care and without a trace of scorn.
21113-wild-bill-s-last-trail:
Ned Buntline, the famous dime novel writer, opens at Laramie. Old scout Sam Chichester meets a passenger off the westbound express: J. B. Hickok, Wild Bill himself. Bill says he is getting toward sunset and will soon pass in his checks. A chill at his heart tells him his time has run out.

Bill has been east with Buffalo Bill and Texas Jack, showing city crowds plains life, and he hated it. A woman there wanted to marry him, though he warned her he might be wiped out any day. Buntline builds the tale toward the famous scout's foretold end.
21205-the-gold-trail:
Harold Bindloss set many novels in western Canada, and this 1910 Grosset and Dunlap tale follows that trail. Chapter titles name a bottomless swamp, a packer, Grenfell's mine, and a copper mine. A character named Stirling, a fiery-tempered railroad builder in the west, drives much of the conflict.

Ida, the heroine, climbs, confides, and asserts her authority as the search for the lode goes on through the ranges. A fruitless search, a rock pool, and a burned clearing mark the party's hard road. Bindloss mixes mining, rail work, and romance into the brisk frontier adventure his readers expected from him.
21216-catharine-s-peril:
Mrs M. E. Bewsher's tale, founded on fact and printed in Edinburgh in 1881, begins in 1812 as Napoleon invades Russia and takes Moscow. Governor Rostopchin resolves to burn the city rather than leave it to the French. Against that fire stands the little Russian girl of the title.

Catharine's peril is being lost in a forest while the world around her burns and armies move. Two shorter stories, The Shabby Surtout and Jane Hill, fill out the volume. Bewsher also wrote The Little Ballet-Girl and The Gipsy's Secret. The book reached its seventh thousand, a sign of steady sales among young readers.
2165-the-lifted-veil:
George Eliot writes a strange, dark tale of a man cursed with foresight and with the power to read other minds. Suffering angina, he knows his end approaches, and he tells how prevision poisoned his life. Eliot published The Lifted Veil in 1859, the year of Adam Bede, as a darker experiment.

The narrator foresees his own death and every misery of his last months, and the gift brings no wisdom, only dread. Eliot's novella stands apart from her realist novels, as a study of a mind too open to others. The tale's foresight, a curse rather than a gift, sets it apart from her realist fiction.
21678-tales-of-giants-from-brazil:
Elsie Spicer Eells retells Brazilian tales in Tales of Giants from Brazil, published in 1918. Helen M. Barton draws the pictures, from a fisherman's son to the Moon Giant. Eells had already issued Fairy Tales from Brazil for young readers.

The Moon Giant woos the giantess of the Great River and wins her love. He builds her a palace of mother-of-pearl where the river meets the sea. Other tales treat the Princess of the Springs, a boy and his violin, and the giant's pupil. Gold, silver, and precious stones deck a set of tales fresh to English children of the day.
21710-the-crew-of-the-water-wagtail:
A ship out of Bristol opens this sea tale by R. M. Ballantyne, set at the start of the sixteenth century. The Water Wagtail sails with a crew that has no idea what dangers wait ahead of them. Paul Burns leads the cast: tall, strong, well read for his day, and hungry for great deeds.

Young Oliver Trench worships Paul and follows him gladly into the voyage. Ballantyne warns readers early that disaster and suffering lie in store for the crew. The story mixes the romance of early ocean travel with storms, strange lands, and hard choices. It shows his fondness for brave crews facing the unknown with faith and nerve.
22205-in-direst-peril:
David Christie Murray opens In Direst Peril with his hero's odd confession. The man is known as Captain Fyffe, though he never held the Queen's commission. He would gladly have fought for his country, he says, but no chance came. Until his marriage, his sword stood at the service of oppressed nationalities instead.

From that start Murray spins an adventure of foreign wars and rescue. Fyffe's career crosses battlefields where small nations fought great empires. Love and honour complicate the fighting in Murray's usual blend. The novel is a rattling specimen of the Victorian adventure tale, written by a man who had covered real wars as a correspondent.
22284-the-forbidden-trail:
Honoré Willsie, who wrote of the desert country she knew, published The Forbidden Trail in 1919. Her trail lifts zig-zag over the Coyote Range in the frontispiece. Roger, the boy at the story's start, has a face of the thinking, dreaming type: long thin jaw, thoughtful mouth, and high forehead. Beauty is seldom intelligent, the narrator remarks, and Roger is no beauty.

Willsie sets her engineers and dreamers in the Arizona desert, where a trail can be forbidden by water, law, or older claims. Her desert books mix surveying, romance, and the fight over western land. This novel, one of her best known, carries the Moral uplift of her work into hard country.
22311-followers-of-the-trail:
Zoe Meyer wrote Followers of the Trail, published in 1926. The book turns to the deep northern woods for its subject. Dark spruce and hemlock guard the secrets of the trail there.

Wild creatures in that green wilderness still know little of man. They regard him, Meyer writes, with more curiosity than fear. The book follows those animals on their own ground. Readers learn how they live, move, and survive in the forest. It belongs to a time when nature writing brought remote woods to city readers. Its appeal rests on close watching and respect for wild life left alone.
22456-the-aeneid-of-virgil:
J. W. Mackail translated Virgil's Aeneid into English prose. The Aeneid tells how Aeneas flees burning Troy to found Rome's line. Juno's hatred of Troy drives much of the poem's trouble.

Juno had heard a race would issue from Trojan blood. That people would one day overthrow her Tyrian citadel, Carthage. Lord of lands and tyrannous in war, they would destroy Libya. So rolled the destinies, Mackail renders the famous line. His translation served generations of students meeting Virgil in English. It keeps the epic's sweep while reading as clear prose. Readers get Rome's founding myth in a scholar's careful, dignified version.
24093-the-root-of-evil:
Thomas Dixon, author of The Leopard's Spots and The Clansman, published this novel in 1911 with Doubleday, Page and Company, illustrated by George Wright. It opens in a city square on a bright morning, where a young lawyer walks in a glow of secret joy, hearing street cries, sparrows, and children as if they were music. Even the roar of trains and rivet hammers across the avenue cannot break his mood.

The novel follows that young lawyer as private happiness meets the harder pressures of city life, ambition, and money. Dixon sets tender feeling against the steel and noise of a rising industrial firm, the American Chemical Company, whose warehouse climbs across the street. Readers get a turn-of-the-century city story about love, work, and the price of getting ahead.
24148-waring-s-peril:
Captain Charles King, of the United States Army, wrote this military novel, published in Philadelphia in 1894. It opens with Lieutenant Waring oversleeping in his quarters, scolding his servant Ananias for letting the guard mounting pass. Waring then borrows a new silk hat from Mr. Larkin, a suit from Mr. Ferry, and a silk umbrella from Mr. Pierce, all for a morning of pleasure.

Waring plans to skip drill for X Battery, breakfast at Moreau's at eleven, and take in the matinée, until word comes of a full review at nine. King, himself a soldier author, tells the tale with barrack-room humor. Readers get a light army story of a gay young officer and the scrapes his easy ways invite.
24274-the-native-soil:
Alan E. Nourse wrote this science fiction story about Venus, the planet of mystery. Before any ship landed, thinkers argued whether its clouded surface hid a steaming jungle, an arid desert of wind-carved sandstone, or an ocean world with giant serpents. When the first Earth ship landed, it found only mud, warm, wet, and clinging, gray, black, brown, yellow, green, blue, and purple.

Venusian plants grow out of the mud, small natives live down in it, and steam rises while rain falls, until the planet seems merely messy. Then technologists of Piper Pharmaceuticals find something growing in that mud besides natives, and the Home Office buys full exploratory and mining rights for a brazen steal. Readers get a sharp satire of speculation and corporate greed.
24337-capitola-s-peril:
Mrs. E. D. E. N. Southworth, author of Ishmael, Self-Raised, and Cruel as the Grave, wrote this sensation novel, published by A. L. Burt Company in New York as a sequel to The Hidden Hand. Its Burns epigraph warns of a night when a child might understand the devil had business on his hand. Chapters follow the orphan's trial, old Hurricane storms, Cap's visit to the hidden house, and the hidden hollow.

Later chapters bring the inmate of the hidden house, Cap freeing the captive, and Cap in captivity. An unexpected visitor at Marah's cottage leads to Black Donald, glory, and Cap captivating a craven. Cap's rage, Capitola capping the climax, and Black Donald's last attempt lead to the awful peril of Capitola, a court-martial, a verdict, a mysterious maniac, and Capitola a capitalist. Readers get a breathless Victorian thriller of a bold heroine.
24695-the-snowshoe-trail:
Edison Marshall wrote this northern adventure, published at New York in 1921 with a frontispiece by Marshall Frantz. He dedicated it to Agnes of the South, calling it a story of the North. It opens at twilight above Bradleyburg, where forest folk pause on a hill to look down on a shadowed street, a mouldering church spire, and unpainted shacks.

An old bull moose in rutting season used to pause there too, mystified by the town's dim lights. Marshall's tale follows trappers, hunters, and wild creatures through snow and forest. Readers get a stirring northern story, full of winter, wilderness, and the pull between town and wild.
24814-the-forest-exiles-the-perils-of-a-:
Captain Mayne Reid wrote The Forest Exiles about a family driven into the forests of Peru, a tale set in the early 1800s. Beneath the adventure runs a full course in the natural history of the region. Each chapter takes up some beast, plant, or craft of the Amazon woods, from the silk-cotton ceiba tree to the blow-gun and its poisoned arrows.

Reid speaks straight to his boy reader, inviting him to travel again and learn nature's lore as they go. The exiles build palm and cane shelters, learn to use native tools, and read the forest as a living book. The story still charms readers who like adventure mixed with real knowledge of the wild.
2535-openings-in-the-old-trail:
Bret Harte gathers nine California stories in this volume, opening with a boy sheltering from high noon heat on Casket Ridge. Colonel Starbottle pleads a case, a hotel landlord rules his house, and a Buckeye heir puzzles over a strange inheritance in the tales that follow.

Smith returns in a new form, Lanty Foster blunders, and an Ali Baba of the Sierras hunts treasure, while Miss Peggy's charges and a goddess of Excelsior close the set. Harte mixes mining camp humor with sudden pathos, and his old trail feels lived in. The book offers the West in small, sharp scenes rather than one long saga.
25383-boy-life-stories-and-readings-sele:
Boy Life, selected from William Dean Howells and arranged by Percival Chubb, was published by Harper and Brothers in 1909. Chubb, director of English at New York's Ethical Culture School, chose the pieces for supplementary reading in elementary schools.

Adventures in a Boy's Town include Pony Baker nearly running off with a circus, a circus magician, and Jim Leonard's hair-breadth escape. A friendship passage praises a wholly innocent bond between two boys, one of them ignorant and idle, loved for his natural good. Howells's American boyhood shines through every page.
26421-great-men-and-famous-women-vol-1-a:
Edited by Charles F. Horne and published by Selmar Hess in 1894, this first volume offers pen-and-pencil sketches of more than two hundred of history's most prominent figures. Contributors include Archdeacon Farrar on Alaric and Attila, Charlotte M. Yonge on Belisarius, H. Rider Haggard on Cortes, and Thomas Carlyle on Olaf Tryggveson, each sketch paired with a portrait.

The contents run from Nebuchadnezzar and Cyrus through Alexander, Hannibal, Caesar, and Charlemagne to Drake, Raleigh, and Miles Standish, mixing rulers, conquerors, and saints of war. Short lives, vivid anecdotes, and moral judgment mark the style, as when Norse bonder-farmers fall silent before Olaf's preaching and accept baptism. Later volumes continue the series through other ages.
26422-great-men-and-famous-women-vol-2-a:
The second volume of Selmar Hess's 1894 series, edited by Charles F. Horne, gathers the soldiers and sea captains of history. Turenne, Marlborough, Prince Eugene, Frederick the Great, and Charles XII of Sweden lead the land commanders, while Napoleon, Ney, Wellington, and Moltke carry the story into modern war. American figures stand thick: Washington's generals, Grant, Lee, Jackson, Sherman, and Sheridan.

Sailors get equal honor, with Nelson, Paul Jones, Decatur, Perry, Farragut, Porter, and Dewey, whose sketch comes from General Joseph Wheeler. Putnam's retreat through the Jerseys in January 1777, after the abandonment of New York, shows the volume's method: a campaign told through a life. Each sketch is brief, stirring, and illustrated, with letters, such as Lee's on duty, adding a personal voice.
26423-great-men-and-famous-women-vol-3-a:
The third volume of Selmar Hess's 1894 series, edited by Charles F. Horne, sketches rulers, saints, thinkers, and reformers of the ancient and early modern world. Moses, David, Lycurgus, Aristotle, Cicero, and Archimedes open the roll, followed by church fathers such as Ambrose and Augustine of Hippo. Later sketches treat Justinian, Alfred the Great, and the monastic schools that kept books and learning alive.

Reformers and monarchs dominate the second half, with Luther, Calvin, Knox, and John Huss beside Charles I, Elizabeth, Isabella of Castile, and Cromwell, whose sketch draws on Macaulay. Copernicus and Galileo represent the new science, while Francis Bacon closes the age of learning. Each life is short, vivid, and paired with a portrait.
26424-great-men-and-famous-women-vol-4-a:
The fourth volume of Selmar Hess's 1894 series, edited by Charles F. Horne, turns from warriors to statesmen, scientists, and founders. John Adams, Franklin, Jefferson, Hamilton, and Lincoln anchor the American roll, with Washington's era seen through letters and lives. European statesmen include Bismarck, Bolivar, Burke, Mirabeau, Robespierre, Gladstone, and Disraeli.

Science and learning claim their own: Newton, Cuvier, Darwin, Humboldt, Agassiz, Champollion, and Pestalozzi, whose sketch comes from Harriet Martineau. One sketch follows a man made baron and president of the Committee of the Interior, whose grasp of affairs and memory won universal admiration. Portraits and short, pointed lives keep the volume's pace brisk across four centuries of public life.
26745-travels-in-peru-on-the-coast-in-th:
Tschudi wrote these travels in Peru, translated from the German by Thomasina Ross and published complete in one volume by A. S. Barnes and Company at New York in 1854. The work joins extracts from Tschudi's journal with his recollections and observations, without chronological order, since zoological work often kept him in one district or hurried him over vast tracts.

Tschudi disclaims travelling romance and confines himself to plain description of facts within his own observation, with pictures of nature in the manner of Buffon. After Lima, oldest and most interesting of Spanish-founded cities on South America's west coast, he crosses ground no European traveller had trodden. He visits the Western Sierra, the Cordilleras, deep Andean valleys, and vast primeval forests. Earthquakes, whose shocks spread north and south from Lima but barely reach the mountains, show his naturalist's eye.
27150-penny-of-top-hill-trail:
Belle Kanaris Maniates's Penny of Top Hill Trail, published in Chicago in 1919, follows Penny among ranch folk, dances, and kittens. The frontispiece shows Penny and the sheriff matching wits under the stars, and the talk runs to fiddlers Sleepy Sandy and Jakey Fourr.

Betty stays up for three dances, Gene Dossey plays gal when partners fail, and kittens must be put down before their eyes open past the nine-day limit. Maniates, author of Amarilly of Clothes-Line Alley, writes a warm, funny ranch story for young readers. The book was published February 8, 1919, with a second printing two days later. The book runs to sixteen chapters.
27616-the-vanishing-race-the-last-great-:
Dr. Joseph K. Dixon published this record in picture and story of the last great Indian council with Doubleday, Page of Garden City, New York, in 1913. Eminent Indian chiefs from nearly every Indian reservation in the United States took part.

Dixon gives the story of their lives as told by themselves, with their speeches and folklore tales, their solemn farewell, and the Indians' story of the Custer fight. Illustrations include the approach of the chiefs, the lone tepee, singing to the spirits, the smoke signal and its answer, and buffalo thundering across the plains. Dixon dedicates the book to his brother the Indian, child of mountain and plain.
27618-the-end-of-a-coil:
Susan Warner, author of The Wide, Wide World, published this novel with James Nisbet in London. Warner tells readers that, as in her My Desire, the turning facts of the story are true, even where they seem most romantic and unlikely.

Chapters follow Dolly's arrival, Christina and her mother, the marine dictionary, and the Achilles, through a piece of rope and the end of school term. Later come London, the peacocks, Brierley Cottage, a consul's office, and a fight, then Limburg, Venice, Naples, and Sorrento. The story opens at an open door of a handsome house in Walnut Street. Warner builds fiction on a factual frame.
27733-through-siberia-and-manchuria-by-r:
Oliver G. Ready wrote this short 1904 account of his rail journey from London to Shanghai across Siberia, a trip he began on October 15, 1903. He first meant the account for friends only, then published it when war broke out between Russia and Japan.

Ready admits that much of what he describes was seen from a moving train window, so detail is limited. Still, his notes on stations, fellow travelers, and the vast country crossed give a firsthand glimpse of the longest railway in the world just before it closed to international traffic.
28156-minor-detail:
Jack Sharkey's Minor Detail is a short science-fiction tale about a grand plan with one fatal flaw. General Smiley Webb has a magnificent idea for landing ground forces in enemy land despite rockets and missiles. The Secretary of Defense, James Whitlow, flies in from the new Capitol in Denver to hear it, briefcase in hand, past reporters and barbed wire.

Webb promises amazement, and his scheme sounds perfect until a single small detail undoes it. Sharkey tells the joke with dry humour, poking at generals, officials, and a nation soothed by slogans. The tale is brief, sharp, and a good sample of 1950s magazine science fiction.
28158-history-of-the-war-in-south-africa:
History of the War in South Africa, 1899-1902, volume one, London, 1906, is the official British history of the Boer War, compiled by direction of His Majesty's Government. Major-General Sir Frederick Maurice, with a staff of officers, took the history over from Colonel Henderson in July 1903 and recast the whole volume after delays over its first chapter.

Chapters cover preparation for war, the outbreak, the theatre of war, and both armies, then the early battles: Talana Hill, Dundee, Elandslaagte, and Lombards Kop. Maurice writes with maps, orders, and official care. The volume gives a solid, if official, account of the war's opening months.
28273-the-cruise-of-the-betsey-or-a-summ:
Hugh Miller wrote The Cruise of the Betsey in 1862 as a summer ramble among the fossil deposits of the Hebrides, with Rambles of a Geologist over ten thousand miles of Scotland. Miller, author of The Old Red Sandstone, died in 1857, and his widow brought this posthumous volume to Gould and Lincoln, his authorized American publishers. The preface recalls Miller's overworked brain and his death.

Miller walks shores, quarries, and islands, reading rocks for ancient seas and creatures. His prose is vivid and personal, mixing geology with travel. The book offers a classic Victorian field journal, where a stonemason turned geologist reads Scotland's past.
28292-ralph-on-the-engine-or-the-young-f:
Allen Chapman wrote Ralph on the Engine in 1909 as the third book in his Railroad Series, following Ralph of the Roundhouse and Ralph in the Switch Tower. Ralph, young fireman of the Limited Mail, faces a night run, a landslide, and a locomotive settled back on a slant, pictured at the front. Grosset and Dunlap published the illustrated volume.

Chapters follow an old-time enemy, hidden plunder, a kidnapping, a railroad strike, runaway trains, and lost diamonds, ending with justice at last. Ralph's work, friends, and foes fill the tale. Boys who love trains get a brisk, old-fashioned railroad adventure.
28455-great-men-and-famous-women-vol-5-a:
Volume V of Great Men and Famous Women, edited by Charles F. Horne and copyrighted in 1894, sketches more than two hundred prominent personages across history, this time reaching back to legend and the ancient world. The frontispiece shows Columbus before Isabella, by Vacslav Brozik.

Subjects include Aeneas, Ulysses, Theseus, Siegfried, King Arthur, Roland, the Cid, Robert Bruce, Joan of Arc, Mary Queen of Scots, and Zenobia, queen of Palmyra. Later figures include Gutenberg, Caxton, Columbus, Vasco da Gama, Captain Cook, Marco Polo, and Captain John Smith. Photogravures and wood engravings illustrate each compact life.
28456-great-men-and-famous-women-vol-6-a:
Great Men and Famous Women, Volume VI, edited by Charles F. Horne and copyrighted in 1894, collects pen-and-pencil sketches of prominent figures in history. The series promised lives of more than two hundred personages, told by many different writers and illustrated with portraits.

This volume includes Benedict Arnold, Nathan Hale, Charlotte Corday, Marie Antoinette, Queen Victoria, and Madame Roland, alongside inventors and explorers such as Edison, Morse, Fulton, Jenner, Pasteur, Livingstone, and Stanley. Generals Custer, Gordon, and Fremont also appear. Each sketch gives a compact life, making the volume a Victorian gallery of heroes, villains, and makers.
28638-rimrock-trail:
J. Allan Dunn's Rimrock Trail, published by A. L. Burt of New York by arrangement with Bobbs-Merrill, opens on a Sunday afternoon at the Three Star rancheria. Mormon Peters, Sandy Bourke cleaning a revolver, and Soda-Water Sam on his harmonica debate Arizona's three C's: climate, cactus, cattle, and coyotes, making four. Sam retorts that Arizona cannot be spelled with a C, any more than Africa with a Z for zebras.

A Boston professor hunting Lost Tribes among cliff dwellers supplies the camp's joke, calling lunch a collation and a napkin a serviette. Chapters follow Grit, Casey, Molly, Sandy calling the turn, Paso Cabras, Bolsa Gap, pay dirt, white gold, a broken rope, and Casey Town. A girl drooped from a long climb pictures the trail's hard end.
28741-the-young-alaskans-on-the-trail:
Emerson Hough wrote this 1911 boys' adventure, the second Young Alaskans book, published by Harper and Brothers. The young heroes take the trail through the gate of the mountains, cross the great divide and the height of land, and follow Mackenzie's route north. Chapters bring a bighorn hunt, a night in the mountains, a caribou hunt, a grizzly hunt, a moose hunt, and steamboating in the far north.

Hough, author of The Story of the Cowboy, fills the journey with camp-fire talk, lessons in wild life, and Native lore, including how the ermine got his black tail. The book teaches woodcraft while it entertains, and its pictures show the boys around the fire. Young readers get a sturdy period adventure of the Canadian north, written by a man who knew the trails he described.
28997-great-men-and-famous-women-vol-7-a:
Charles F. Horne edited this 1894 volume, the seventh of Great Men and Famous Women, a series of pen and pencil sketches of more than two hundred prominent persons in history. The volume's contents include Robert Browning, William Cullen Bryant, John Bunyan, Robert Burns, Thomas Carlyle, Cervantes, Thomas Chatterton, Geoffrey Chaucer, and James Fenimore Cooper.

Each life gets a short sketch by a named author, with pictures, including the first meeting of Dante and Beatrice as frontispiece. The series aimed to give general readers vivid lives of famous men and women in brief compass. Readers get a Victorian who's who in story form, useful for browsing and for first meetings with great names.
29183-partners-of-the-out-trail:
Harold Bindloss published this adventure novel in 1919, in England under the title Dearham's Inheritance. Part one, The Linesman, follows Jim, a man working a telegraph line through snow country, after a wire breaks. A third partner joins him on the trail, and the chapters move through watches, councils, rapids, and fire.

Part two, The Landowner, brings Jim home to guests, ponds, fences, and old men's whims, as inheritance and rivalry reshape his life. Bindloss writes with the steady pace of the northern adventure tale: hard work, open country, and loyalty tested. Readers get a long, sturdy novel of the Canadian-style frontier, in two halves that mirror each other.
29352-great-men-and-famous-women-vol-8-a:
Charles F. Horne edited this eighth volume of Great Men and Famous Women, a series of pen and pencil sketches of more than two hundred prominent personages in history. Selmar Hess published the volume in New York in 1894, with illustrations and wood engravings. Each sketch pairs a life with a portrait or scene.

Volume eight leans toward artists and performers. Contents include Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo by Anna Jameson, Beethoven, Sarah Bernhardt as Cleopatra, Rosa Bonheur, Edwin Booth, and Charlotte Cushman. William Hogarth, Paganini, Giuseppe Verdi, Gustave Dore, and Benjamin West also appear. Readers get a Victorian gallery of genius, brisk and illustrated, for browsing or for first acquaintance.
29543-ox-team-days-on-the-oregon-trail:
Ezra Meeker, in collaboration with Howard R. Driggs, wrote this 1927 book in the Pioneer Life Series from World Book Company, retracing the journey of Meeker's youth by ox team. Drawings by F. N. Wilson and photographs illustrate a trek from Ohio to the coast, told in parts that begin with back to beginnings and boyhood days in old Indiana. Meeker retraced the trail so Americans might ever know where the pioneers' footsteps led.

The book mixes memoir, history, and tribute, honoring the heroic toil of those who crossed plains and mountains by wagon. Its tone is earnest and patriotic, in the manner of its age. Readers of western and pioneer history will find a first-hand, heartfelt account of the Oregon Trail from one who walked it young and retraced it old.
29771-the-planetoid-of-peril:
Paul Ernst first printed this short tale in Astounding Stories in November 1931. Harley 2Q14N20, a lone prospector, stops outside the dome of the Celestial Developments Company, a firm set up in 2045 that sells choice asteroids to the rich. One blank space on its chart marks an unsold rock, Asteroid Z-40, and wild tales say an unkillable being lives on it.

Harley, who cannot pay the firm's price, sets out alone to face and master what waits there. The tale plays on the gap between the firm's glossy sales talk and the cold facts of a small rock in space. It is a brisk space yarn of one man's nerve, a strange foe, and a claim staked where no buyer with deep pockets dared to go.
29829-hair-breadth-escapes-perilous-inci:
T. S. Arthur collected these perilous incidents in the lives of sailors and travellers, printed in New York in 1889. Seven tales make up the book. They are Pirate Life, Captivity among the Japanese, and A Sea-Fight on the Cuban Coast. A Winter in the Frozen Ocean, The Shipwreck, and Voyage to the East Indies follow. Home-Sickness of a Siberian closes the set. Each turns on a narrow escape, told in the first person.

Pirate Life opens on the merchant vessel Dolphin, bound from Jamaica for London. The assistant pilot spots a suspicious schooner off Cuba and warns the captain, a man of arrogance, avarice, and obstinacy. The captain scorns the counsel, trusting the English flag, until the strange deck swarms with armed men and boats are lowered. Arthur keeps the peril plain and the pace fast, in the style of a sailor's yarn book.
30212-the-great-cattle-trail:
Edward S. Ellis opens his Forest and Prairie Series with a cattle-trail adventure, published by the John C. Winston Company under a copyright of 1894. A race for life fronts the book. Chapters move from the ranch through an alarming interruption, just in time, and a desperate venture, to upstairs and downstairs and Dinah's discovery and exploit. The mesquite bush, a surprise, changing places, a roof, and a dead race follow, with a friend in need and a vanishing.

Later chapters bring the boys' arrival, a passage through the bush, Thunderbolt, a good-by, and a strange delay before the trail heads northward. A shot from the darkness, Shackaye the Comanche, a mishap, old acquaintances, and a stand at bay lead to a flag of truce, diplomacy, and a flank movement. Ellis, author of the Wyoming, Log Cabin, and Deerfoot series, writes for young readers who like western action.
30324-the-pathless-trail:
Arthur O. Friel tells The Pathless Trail, published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York under a 1922 copyright by Harper and Brothers. Sons of the north open, with at sundown, the voice of the wilds, the German, into the bush, and in the night watch. Cold steel, the double-cross, fiddlers three, and by the light of storm follow. 

Mud sucks at the ankles of three men on a jungle river's shore as they watch a smoke ribbon drift apart above the trees to the northwest. Different in type, all three were cradled in the same far northern land. The tallest, lean but broad-shouldered, dark-haired and gray-eyed, stands soldierly and unmoved. His two mates betray their thoughts in blue eyes: the stocky red-headed one, and the slender blond one, bronzed by the sun.
30925-the-wilderness-trail:
Frank Williams, whose full name was Francis William Sullivan, wrote this 1913 wilderness adventure for Grosset and Dunlap in New York, with pictures by Douglas Duer. Its twenty-six chapters run from Up for Judgment and Ill Report through a mysterious message, the danger zone, a death trail, and a last stand. They close with a forced march, awaiting the hangman, secreted evidence, and renunciation. Jean, Maria, and other figures move through its northern story.

Chapter one opens with Donald McTavish glaring at his superior Fitzpatrick, a white-bearded man in a great chair at the factory. Fitzpatrick accuses no one outright, but says a great quantity of valuable furs trapped in McTavish's district has not been turned in. McTavish was called down by dogs in dead winter to explain the gap. The novel follows that charge through escape, rescue, and fearful odds in the fur country.
31262-rastignac-the-devil:
Philip José Farmer's novella, printed in Fantastic Universe in May 1954, follows Rastignac, a man of New Gaul living deep underground without a Skin, happier than he has been since childhood. After an apocalyptic war, French survivors crowded into the Loire Valley, squeezed between a hostile northern Colossus and a friendly southern confederation. They sent six great ships holding thirty thousand people into interstellar space in the twenty-second century.

More than three hundred and fifty years later, Rastignac wants to leave New Gaul and voyage to the stars. He seeks the Six Bright Stars and his world's eventual freedom from a triangular despotism. The magazine's headnote calls it high-fidelity fiction three centuries into the future, and the tale lives up to that billing with an uneasy sense that it happens somewhere unexplored even today.
31487-boy-scouts-on-the-great-divide-or-:
Archibald Lee Fletcher's Boy Scouts on the Great Divide, or The Ending of the Trail, published by M. A. Donohue and Company of Chicago with copyright in 1913, follows boy scouts across the mountains. Its contents promise a runaway, a case stated, a chase in the night, a detective and a robber, and the call of the beaver. They continue with arrest as spies, a midnight bear hunt, a threatened lynching, a Wyoming hold-up, an interrupted wig-wag, Tommy going after bear steak, and a pair of prisoners.

The trail of the title ends in the high country, where scouting skills meet real danger. Fletcher writes for boys in the scouting-story tradition, with action in every chapter. Readers will find a brisk, outdoor adventure, where signals, tracking, and courage carry the patrol through one danger to another.
31488-the-little-regiment-and-other-epis:
Stephen Crane's The Little Regiment and Other Episodes of the American Civil War, published by D. Appleton and Company with copyright in 1896, gathers six Civil War stories. Alongside the title piece stand "Three Miraculous Soldiers," "A Mystery of Heroism," "An Indiana Campaign," "A Gray Sleeve," and "The Veteran." Crane, author of The Red Badge of Courage and Maggie, writes here in the same stark, impressionistic manner.

The opening story begins in fog, where a column of infantry in heavy overcoats seems a long, low shadow in the mist. Crane's interest is less in strategy than in what battle feels like to ordinary soldiers. Readers of American war fiction will find the collection a sharp companion to his famous novel, with heroism, fear, and chance rendered in brief, vivid episodes.
31759-the-infant-s-skull-or-the-end-of-t:
Eugene Sue's The Infant's Skull, or The End of the World, is a tale of the millennium translated from French by Daniel De Leon and published in 1904. It is part of his Mysteries of the People series. Its translator's preface recalls the historic fear witnessed on the first day of the year 1000, with a second or adjourned catastrophe thirty-two years later.

Part one, The Castle of Compiegne, opens in 987 at the Fountain of the Hinds, where a plainly dressed woman comes to water among stags and hinds. Part two, The End of the World, follows apocalyptic frenzy, starvation, and flight to Anjou. Readers get a historical romance of the year 1000, when many believed the world itself would end.
32333-voyage-of-the-paper-canoe-a-geogra:
Nathaniel H. Bishop's Voyage of the Paper Canoe, a geographical journey of twenty-five hundred miles from Quebec to the Gulf of Mexico, was published by Lee and Shepard in Boston. It carries numerous illustrations and maps specially prepared for the work, priced at two dollars and fifty cents. Bishop also wrote Four Months in a Sneak Box, a boat voyage of twenty-six hundred miles down the Ohio and Mississippi rivers and along the Gulf of Mexico. He writes as a travelling geographer.

His paper canoe carries him from Quebec to the Gulf. The journey is measured in miles and mapped for readers. A frontispiece shows the home of the alligator, and the book's maps and illustrations follow the route. Readers get a Victorian canoe-travel narrative, part geography lesson and part adventure, where a paper boat proves itself over twenty-five hundred miles of river, lake, and gulf.
3247-the-patrol-of-the-sun-dance-trail:
Ralph Connor sets this mounted police tale on the Sun Dance Trail. The trail-runner opens it, with his country's need and a fishing trip. The big chief, the ancient sacrifice, and the illusive copperhead follow, leading to the Sarcee camp and the girl on number one. A ride up the Bow, Raven to the rescue, and Smith's work carry the patrol forward.

In the Sun Dance Canyon and the big wigwam, the story reaches its center, with good man and good squaw as its plain verdict. Connor writes of police, native peoples, and frontier justice with his usual earnestness. Wide country, hard riding, and duty tested where law and custom meet: the Mounted Police romance in full.
32950-camp-and-trail:
Stewart Edward White's Camp and Trail, first issued in book form in 1911 from earlier Outing magazine pieces, is a practical handbook for wilderness travel. Its chapters move in order from the wilderness traveler and common sense in camp to personal gear, camp and cook outfits, food, horse packs, and canoes. Photographs and a frontispiece painting give the advice a visual anchor.

White writes for readers who mean to go out and do it, not merely dream about it. He weighs what to carry, what to leave, how to feed a party, and how to handle horses, mules, and burros on rough ground. The book's lasting appeal lies in that plain, tested counsel, which still reads as a clear guide to an older style of travel by trail and water.
33505-the-trembling-of-the-veil:
W. B. Yeats recalls his early literary life in this privately printed 1922 memoir, issued in a numbered edition of one thousand signed copies. The book opens in Bedford Park, where Yeats's family settled in a red-brick house after arriving from Dublin, and follows his formation through the years 1887 to 1891. Friends, studios, and London literary circles fill the first book.

Later books turn to Ireland after the fall of Parnell, to occult study, to the tragic generation of writers Yeats knew, and to the stirring of the bones of memory itself. The memoir blends personal recollection with literary history, giving an intimate account of how a young Irish poet found his voice among painters, playwrights, and fellow dreamers.
33607-the-mother-of-st-nicholas-a-story-:
Grant Balfour tells a story of duty and peril set in the third century, in Patara on the southwest coast of Asia Minor. The city, famous in sacred legend as the birthplace of the white-haired gift-giver of Christmas, lives under Roman rule while persecution gathers again against its Christians. Prejudice stirs the common people, and officials look the other way as believers are arrested on plausible pretexts.

Fifteen chapters follow the mother of Nicholas through watching enemies, a ministering angel figure, indignation and perplexity among the city's leaders, and waiting for a victim. The climax moves into the amphitheatre and the arena, with a lion and a man with a dagger. The tale links the Christmas saint's origins to the courage of the early church under threat.
34082-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This slice of volume two of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica runs from Aram, Eugene, to Arcueil. Articles treat Aramaic languages, Aranda, the Aran Islands, Aranjuez, Arany, Arapaho, Ararat in mountains and in an Australian town, Araroba powder, Aras, and Arason. Arator, Aratus the statesman and the didactic poet, Araucania, and the Araucanians follow.

Later entries cover Araucaria, Arauco, the Aravalli Hills, Arawak, Arbaces, Arbe, Arbela, Arber, arbitrage, and arbitration, then a long run on arch, archaeology, Archaeopteryx, archaism, and archangel. The slice shows the Britannica's broad alphabetical reach. It serves as a handy sample of geography, history, and science.
3413-the-blazed-trail:
Stewart Edward White sets this novel in the pine forests of the American North, where lumbermen cut timber and surveyors mark new ground. The parts are named for the work itself: the forest, the landlooker, the blazing of the trail, and the following of the trail. Its hero, Thorpe, belongs to the advance guard of pioneers who open country for farms and towns.

White writes the woods with close detail, from snow and rivers to the still pine stands and the prairie edge. The story follows Thorpe's labor, his hopes, and a romance that runs beside the hard work. Readers who like outdoor adventure and stories of how the frontier was cleared will find a sturdy plot and a strong sense of place.
34163-the-roman-poets-of-the-augustan-ag:
W. Y. Sellar wrote this study of Virgil among the Roman poets of the Augustan age. A third edition appeared at Oxford in 1897 by the Clarendon Press, with a first edition in 1877. Sellar was late professor of humanity at Edinburgh and fellow of Oriel College, Oxford. He dedicates the book to E. L. Lushington, late professor of Greek at Glasgow, whose teaching shaped his youth.

Chapters open with a general introduction on the Augustan age's relation to other literary epochs, then follow Virgil's life and work. Sellar joins fine scholarship with a generous love of literature. The book remains a classic study of Virgil and his age.
4363-beyond-good-and-evil:
Friedrich Nietzsche wrote this book as a prelude to a philosophy of the future, translated here by Helen Zimmern from the Complete Works edition of 1909 to 1913. Its chapters treat the prejudices of philosophers, the free spirit, the religious mood, and the natural history of morals. Later chapters cover scholars, virtues, peoples, and what is noble.

Nietzsche attacks the idea that philosophy stands above life, and he probes the drives behind truth, morality, and religion. Aphorisms and interludes break the argument into sharp fragments. The book is demanding but central, and this translation keeps Zimmern's early English, with modernized spellings of today and tomorrow.
4605-basil:
Wilkie Collins dedicated Basil to his old friend Charles James Ward, and he says the main event of the story rests on a fact within his own knowledge. Where he shaped that fact into narrative, he tried to keep it touching on something real and true, whether from his own experience or from stories told to him. The novel runs in three parts, and it belongs to the early Victorian sensation school Collins helped to create.

Basil, a young gentleman, marries in secret below his rank, and the marriage drags him into family rage, shame, and revenge. Collins builds suspense through letters, confessions, and confrontations, while keeping a close eye on class and respectability. Readers get a gripping early sensation novel, darker and more personal than a simple mystery, about a rash promise and the long price it exacts.
4684-the-u-p-trail:
Zane Grey's The U. P. Trail takes the building of the Union Pacific railroad as its epic subject. Grey opens by marvelling at how the line was pushed through unwatered wilderness and haunts of savage tribes. At each stage of construction, roaring, impromptu cities full of gold, lust, and death sprang up, then died away, leaving only wayside stations in the desert.

Chinese workers laboured beside border ruffians and broken men from Europe, gambling, drinking, quarrelling, and murdering like wolves. Yet the whole turmoil was directed by gentlemen in frock-coats, seeking a fortune and a later visit to Paris. Grey treats the railroad as the typical achievement of its age, joining all ranks and all ends of the world in one plot. Readers get a big western novel of iron, gold, and human ambition.
5067-the-rainbow-trail:
Zane Grey's Rainbow Trail returns to the desert country of Riders of the Purple Sage, answering a question readers often asked about that romance's ending. Grey opens with the desert's spell returning: veils like purple smoke in the canyon, silence, and the strange wild life of the last American wilderness, wild still almost as it ever was.

The story follows the trail to the foot of the rainbow, through the Grand Canyon of the Colorado to Willow Springs, in chapters that mix romance, pursuit, and canyon scenery. Grey notes the tale first appeared serially in a different form. Readers get a western sequel that stands alone, lush with desert color and frontier feeling.
5194-the-ivory-trail:
Talbot Mundy's Ivory Trail opens with a song of Zanzibar, greener than emeralds and whiter than diamonds. It follows ivory hunters and adventurers into East Africa. Chapters move through slave gangs, a great game reserve, and songs of elephants and dark lords, as the trail leads inland toward fortune and danger.

Mundy writes of the ivory trade, its hunters, traders, and porters, with the pace of popular adventure. The novel offers a vivid, if dated, picture of early twentieth-century Africa as imagined by a writer who knew the region's stories well. It remains one of his best known African tales.
5233-the-iron-trail:
Rex Beach's Iron Trail is set in Alaska. A tide, a girl appearing out of the night, and an Irish prince open a story of railroads and rivalry. Chapters follow a journey to Hope, the dreamer and his dream, the villain Curtis Gordon. The novel explores Eliza Violet Appleton's two sides, toward a battle at Gordon's crossing.

Beach mixes frontier adventure with business intrigue, as men fight over a railway route through wild country. The novel offers readers the Alaska of the gold-rush era, with storms, camps. Strong personalities carry the story, told at the brisk pace of popular adventure fiction.
5718-the-great-salt-lake-trail:
Colonel Henry Inman traces the history of the trail to the Great Salt Lake through explorers, trappers, traders, and soldiers. Chapters cover expeditions from 1774 onward. They treat the old trappers and their outfits, trading posts, and the Mormons. They also treat the Pony Express, the stage route to the Pacific, and the Union Pacific Railroad. Later chapters turn to Sioux traditions, the Crows, Blackfeet lore, Buffalo Bill, and Custer's command.

The book works as a fireside history, gathering camp stories, local color, and frontier incident into one long narrative. Readers meet Jim Beckwourth, Kit Carson, and many lesser-known guides, and they see how a trail became a road, then a railroad. It suits readers of western history who enjoy anecdote-rich storytelling alongside the larger sweep of settlement.
6715-isobel-a-romance-of-the-northern-tr:
James Oliver Curwood sets Isobel on the northern trail, a thousand miles north of civilization at Point Fullerton. Sergeant William MacVeigh of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police writes his half-year report with a pencil stub. He hunts Scottie Deane, a murderer, for three hundred miles along Hudson's Bay. His search runs to Eskimo Point and north to Wagner Inlet. Hope has not left him yet.

Into that harsh hunt comes Isobel, and love grows where law and cold rule. Curwood writes with a northerner's love of snow, dogs, and lonely trails. Isobel is a stirring, romantic tale of the far north, where duty and heart pull a mounted policeman two ways.
6905-the-boy-aviators-in-africa-or-an-ae:
Captain Wilbur Lawton sends his boy aviators to Africa on an aerial ivory trail, opening with a reunion and a cache of stolen ivory. Harry, Billy Barnes the reporter, and their chums pack, quarrel, and joke as they set out, warned to be serious about the work ahead. The contents promise a witch doctor, a pool of death, a traitor in camp, and a battle in the air.

Slave traders, gorillas with an aerial tow line, a rogue elephant, and an Arab chief test the boys in turn. Friends in need, a smoke reader, and a rescue by aeroplane carry the tale toward its close aboard the Brigand. Lawton keeps the tone brisk and boyish, with flight as the answer to nearly every peril on the ground.
6906-the-lost-trail:
Edward Ellis opens this frontier tale in early spring, with Jack Carleton, a sturdy youth of seventeen, following a clear trail through western Kentucky toward the Mississippi. Mile by mile he tracks the spaced marks, until an enemy in a tree and a rifle shot break the quiet. Chapters carry him to the river bank, a visitor from the far shore, and nights around the camp fire.

Deerfoot, the skilled woodsman of the chapter titles, shapes much of the action, from a surprised fisherman to maneuvers, messages, and a fort in the trees. The tale moves through pursuits, wigwams, and turning tables, with a stranger, a smoke signal, and a farewell at the close. It is a brisk story of trail craft and nerve.
6979-the-little-regiment-and-other-episo:
Stephen Crane gathers Civil War episodes here, led by The Little Regiment, with Three Miraculous Soldiers, A Mystery of Heroism, An Indiana Campaign, A Grey Sleeve, and The Veteran. The title story opens in fog, where a column's heavy overcoats take a pale blue hue and the regiment seems a long low shadow in the mist. Above the thick ranks a muttering, part grumble and part joke, blends into the voice of the column.

Across a little river a town looms spectral on grey cloud masses, while guns on the northern bank have battered a belfry into dim sight. Crane writes war as men feel it, in color, sound, and fear, rather than as generals plan it. The stories that follow keep that hard, close focus on soldiers under fire.
7346-among-malay-pirates-a-tale-of-adven:
G. A. Henty's Among Malay Pirates opens with Harry Parkhurst, a midshipman of sixteen, leaning on the rail of Her Majesty's gunboat Serpent with his chum Dick Balderson, staring gloomily at a turbid stream. One day is just like another, Harry complains. Perspiration runs from morning to night, mist lies on the water, and only a run out every three or four days brings fresh air, lest fever eat them up.

Pirates soon break the dull routine, and the gunboat's boys face adventure and peril in Malay waters. Henty writes brisk naval adventure, with heat, boredom, and sudden action in equal share. Young readers get a sea tale where patience snaps into danger without warning.
7537-shallow-soil:
Knut Hamsun, the Norwegian novelist who would win the Nobel Prize, writes of a land and a boy shaped by it. This is the authorized translation by Carl Christian Hyllested. The translator's preface recalls the stir of Hamsun's first autobiographical chapters. They appeared in a Danish magazine in the autumn of 1888, when Ibsen, Björnson, Brandes, and Strindberg stood at the height of their European fame.

The world of the novel is Norway's rugged coast, a drama in granite flung far into the Arctic night. There a taciturn, peculiar lad grows up inured to hardship and danger, in close communion with nature, dreaming through the endless northern twilight and reveling through the brief, intense summer. Shallow Soil gives English readers Hamsun's northern ground: hard, beautiful, and unforgiving.
896-the-jubilee-of-the-constitution-deli:
John Quincy Adams delivered this oration on 30 April 1839, before the New York Historical Society, to mark the jubilee of the Constitution. Fifty years after Washington's first inauguration, Adams asks his fellow citizens to recall the founding act, its authors, and the Union it made, and to weigh what it still demands.

Adams speaks as a former president and a son of a founder, with learning and moral gravity. His oration praises the Constitution as a living bond, not a dead letter, and warns against forgetting its spirit. The text is a key document of American civic oratory, and of Adams's late public voice.
9857-the-long-labrador-trail:
Dillon Wallace wrote The Long Labrador Trail in 1917, a true tale of travel through Labrador's wilds. Wallace, famed for The Lure of the Labrador Wild, dedicates the book to his wife's memory. Chapters follow the voice of the wilderness, the old Indian trail, and Lake Nipishish, toward Seal Lake and Michikamau. A parting, a northern divide, and disaster in the rapids follow.

Later chapters bring tidewater posts, Eskimo camps, Arctic ice, and a sledge journey across the barrens. Wallace writes with hardy, plain detail. A reader gets a gripping northern travel book, rich in trails, lakes, and the endurance of men and dogs.
9932-the-last-trail:
Zane Grey's 1909 frontier novel opens at dusk in the wild Ohio valley, where a traveler on the river trail hopes to reach Fort Henry that night. His guide has abandoned him, his teamster is new to the frontier, and the forest trail grows hard to follow.

From that anxious start, Grey builds a story of wilderness travel, Indian danger, and frontier courage, in the land of his earlier border tales. His eye for rivers, forests, and lonely trails gives the book its force. Readers get a classic western of the Ohio country, when the frontier was still raw and thinly held.
a-holiday-in-the-happy-valley-with-pen-a: Thomas Robert Swinburne takes a holiday in the happy valley with pen and pencil. His illustrated journey visits Srinagar, the Jhelum, the Dal Lake, and Udaipur in Kashmir. Colored illustrations show byways, bunds, boats, and mountain tarns. Swinburne writes and draws a traveler's portrait of Kashmir in early spring. The pen and pencil work makes Kashmir feel near and real.
a-new-conscience-and-an-ancient-evil: Jane Addams examines the ancient evil of her title, the traffic in women that large cities preferred not to name, in this Hull House study. Drawing on material gathered by the Juvenile Protective Association of Chicago, she argues that a new public conscience must replace silence about women cast out as outcasts. She moves through legal enactments, economic conditions, moral education, rescue work, and increased social control as remedies.
among-malay-pirates-a-tale-of-adventure-:
G. A. Henty wrote Among Malay Pirates as a tale of adventure and peril for boy readers, and it opens aboard Her Majesty's gunboat Serpent in hot, feverish river country. Midshipmen Harry Parkhurst and Dick Balderson, both about sixteen, are bored with anchor duty and longing for something to happen among the passing canoes and dhows.

Something does: the river world they watch, of traders, chiefs, and pirate crews, turns dangerous, and the boys are drawn into captures, escapes, and fighting up-country. Henty mixes naval routine, local color as his age saw it, and steady doses of peril to keep his young heroes earning their keep. It is empire-era adventure fiction in his standard, much-reprinted mould.
basil: Basil, Wilkie Collins's novel. The young hero's tale. This book preserves that story. It awaits future readers. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The paper lived through the years.
beyond-good-and-evil:
Friedrich Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil appears here in the English translation by Helen Zimmern. Nietzsche opens with a preface mocking dogmatic philosophers, thinkers who claim final systems of truth. He calls Plato's pure spirit and absolute good a noble error now happily outgrown. The book that follows is restless, witty, and deliberately unsettling.

Nine chapters move from the prejudices of philosophers to the free spirit and the religious mood. A chapter of aphorisms, short sharp sayings, interrupts the argument. Later parts give a natural history of morals, reflections on scholars, and portraits of peoples and countries. The final chapter asks what nobility means. Nietzsche urges readers to question herd morality, the values of the crowd, and to create values of their own.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-luxe:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Luxeuil describes a monastery in Franche-Comté, the great Irish monk Columbanus founded it in 585 on Luxovium's ruined Roman castle. Named for St. Peter, it soon became Gaul's most famed and great monastery.

The monks were so many that choir followed choir in chanting the Office, and here first sounded the laus perennis, the endless chant day and night. Columbanus' rule, borrowed mostly from Irish houses, did not long prevail, and the entry weighs his forceful, fiery nature against St. Benedict's care. Luxeuil's sway, its rule and its founder's nature form the entry's centre.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albero-de-mon:
Albero de Montreuil was Archbishop of Trier, born near Toul in Lorraine about 1080 and dead at Coblenz in 1152. After holding posts in the churches of Toul and Verdun, he became Archdeacon and Provost of St. Arnulf at Metz. There he joined the church reform party against Bishop Adalbero IV and travelled to Rome in person to seek the bishop's removal by Pope Paschal II.

Back home, Albero helped secure Theotger's election: the Black Forest abbot of St. George took office unwillingly in July 1118. As archbishop he pressed reform with vigour and restored peace and order in his archdiocese. The entry draws on the metrical Deeds of Albero and other medieval histories of Trier.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-rail:
The altar rail guards the sanctuary, separating it from the church's body, and is also called the communion rail, since the faithful kneel there for Holy Communion. Carved wood, metal, marble, or other precious material forms it. It stands about two feet six inches high and six to nine inches wide on top.

A clean white linen cloth, about two feet wide and the rail's full length, spreads before communicants to catch particles falling from the priest's hands. Each communicant holds it under the chin in both hands. Lace or netting would defeat its purpose, though a fine lace or embroidered border is allowed. A gilt paten, salver, or larger pall may replace the cloth, passed along the rail, never a consecrated paten in lay hands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-gaubi:
Antoine Gaubil, a French Jesuit missionary born in 1689, spent nearly forty years at Peking as astronomer and historian. He reached China in 1722 and stayed until his death, heading a school where Manchus learned Latin for Russian affairs. His Chinese name was Sun Kiun-yung, and his letters reached scholars across Europe.

From Chinese sources he translated a history of Genghis Khan and part of the Tang annals, and he wrote a treatise on Chinese chronology. His study of Chinese astronomy appeared in a Paris collection, and his version of the Book of History followed after his death. The entry calls him the best astronomer and historian among French Jesuits in China of his century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-margi:
Valencia-born Franciscan Antonio Margil, who lived from 1657 to 1726, volunteered for the Indian missions of America after joining his order in 1673 and reaching Vera Cruz in 1683. Stationed at the missionary college of Santa Cruz, Querétaro, he worked across Mexico, Yucatán, Costa Rica, and Nicaragua. Above all he worked in Guatemala, where he earned the name Apostle of Guatemala. He walked barefoot, fasted every day, ate neither meat nor fish, and spent most of the night in prayer.

In 1706 he became first guardian, or head, of the new missionary college of Guadalupe at Zacatecas. Ten years later he led three priests and two lay brothers into Texas, founding missions of Guadalupe among the Nacogdoches, Dolores for the Ays, and San Miguel among other peoples. The article credits his harsh penance and tireless travel with extraordinary success among Indians and colonists alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernardo-buil:
