Bernardo Buil, also spelled Boil or Boyl, a Franciscan friar, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Confusion clouds him because two Spaniards of the name lived at once, one Franciscan and one Benedictine, and some writers merged them into a single man. The entry argues they were distinct.

To the Franciscan, Pope Alexander VI addressed a bull of June 1493 appointing him the pope's first deputy for the New World, the pope's deputy for the newly found lands. He sailed with Columbus's second voyage and quarrelled with the admiral over treatment of the natives. The piece untangles an identity puzzle at the dawn of American missions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brazil:
Brazil, a republic larger than the United States without Alaska and the Philippines, spans 3,218,130 square miles from 5 degrees north to 33 degrees south. It borders every South American country except Chile, with the Amazon basin's low Selvas in the north and west and plateaus of 2,000 to 4,000 feet in the south and east. Its Atlantic coast runs about 4,000 miles, and its rivers rank among the world's greatest travel routes.

Mountain systems include the Serra do Mar, rising to Itatiaia near 10,000 feet, the Serra Central, and a northwestern range dividing the Sao Francisco and Tocantins from the Parana. Later sections cover climate, farming, minerals, manufactures, railroads, commerce, population, government, religion, church organization, schools, and history, giving a full portrait of the young republic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-devil:
A doctrinal entry on the devil, the name commonly given to fallen angels, also called demons. With the definite article it means Lucifer, their chief, as in Matthew's phrase about the devil and his angels. Greek diabolos means slanderer or accuser, matching the Hebrew Satan, an adversary, and the name marks an office, not a nature.

No single passage gives the full teaching: scattered notices from Genesis to Apocalypse must be read together with patristic tradition. The Fourth Lateran Council states the Church line, that devil and demons were created good by God and made themselves evil. Later pages follow the scriptural trail and close with Paul's armour passage, urging truth, justice, peace, and the shield of faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dicuil:
Dicuil was an Irish monk and geographer of the late eighth century. He worked in a monastery of the Frankish kingdom and knew the islands near England and Scotland from his own travel. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows his two surviving works. One is an astronomical computus written between 814 and 816, and the other is a geography finished in 825.

His geography, On the Measurement of the World, drew on a survey ordered by the emperor Theodosius the Second. It also drew on Pliny and Isidore of Seville, while adding what Dicuil had seen himself. The entry gives a clear portrait of a monk who joined book learning to firsthand knowledge of distant shores.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eskil:
Eskil was Archbishop of Lund in Skåne, Sweden, born about 1100 and dead at Clairvaux on 6 September 1181. He was one of Scandinavia's most capable princes of the Church. A man of profound piety, he defended the hierarchy courageously against civil power and clerical usurpers. His father Christian descended from an illustrious Jutland family related to several royal houses.

At twelve Eskil entered the cathedral school at Hildesheim. During a dangerous illness he saw a vision of the Mother of God, who chided his frivolous conduct, saved him, and demanded five measures of corn as a thank-offering. The vision was read to mean he would rise high and establish five confraternities. In 1131 his uncle Asser, first Archbishop of Lund, made him provost of the cathedral. In 1134 he became Bishop of Roskilde, and after Asser's death in 1137 succeeded him as archbishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-etienne-de-ca:
Etienne de Carheil, a French missionary among the Indians of Canada, was born at Carentoir in France in November 1633 and died at Quebec on 27 July 1726. He joined the Society of Jesus at Paris in 1652, studied at Amiens, La Flèche, and Bourges, and taught at Rouen and Tours. Ordained in 1666, he sailed for Canada and spent two years at Quebec preparing for mission work.

He had longed to die for Christ. Instead, thirty years of hardship among the Hurons and Iroquois became his martyrdom in Canada. Cayuga was his first mission, until the chiefs drove him out in 1684. Three years teaching grammar at the College of Quebec followed, and then came his assignment to the Mission of Mackinac. His opposition to the brandy traffic angered La Mothe Cadillac, commandant at Mackinac, and he was compelled to return to Quebec in 1703.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-evil:
Evil, in the large sense used here, is the sum of all that stands against human desires and needs, and hence of the suffering that fills life. The entry first defines its kinds. Physical evil covers sickness, accident, death, poverty, and oppression, and all that thwarts man's powers by nature or by faulty social order. Moral evil is the will turning from the moral order toward ends conscience condemns. Metaphysical evil is the mutual limit of natural things, by which none reaches full perfection, as beasts prey on beasts and storms wreck the order of nature.

The article then argues that all evil is at root negative, a loss or lack of some good needful for perfection, not a thing in itself. Wrong action adds a positive choice, yet its evil lies in turning from right.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fifth-lateran:
The Fifth Lateran Council met at Rome from 1512 to 1517. Pope Julius II called it to answer the rebel cardinals' council at Pisa. Fifteen cardinals, ten archbishops, and fifty-six bishops attended its opening. Leo X continued it to its twelfth session after Julius died in February 1513.

The council finally revoked the Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges in 1516. It approved a new concordat with Francis I of France. It sanctioned montes pietatis, pawn shops for the necessitous poor under strict church control. It also banned printing books without the permission of the diocesan bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-first-lateran:
The First Lateran Council met at Rome in March 1123, under Callistus II in person. It followed the Concordat of Worms of 1122, the first agreement of its kind between pope and emperor. More than three hundred bishops and six hundred abbots assembled for the council. Both originals of the Concordat were read aloud and ratified by the assembly.

The council issued twenty-two disciplinary canons, mostly restating earlier decrees. Clerical marriage was forbidden, and marriages of clerics were declared null by law. Crusaders' families and goods gained safeguards, and lay seizure of church offerings drew excommunication. Abbots were barred from penance, sick visits, and extreme unction, and took their holy oils from their bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fourth-latera:
The Fourth Lateran Council met at Rome in November 1215, summoned by Pope Innocent III, who had planned a general council from the start of his reign. It was huge: seventy-one patriarchs and metropolitans, 412 bishops, and 900 abbots and priors. Envoys came from Emperor Frederick II and the kings of France, England, Aragon, Hungary, Cyprus, and Jerusalem.

The fathers did little more than approve seventy decrees Innocent had already drawn up, but that approval gave them ecumenical force. Canon 1 set out the Catholic faith and the doctrine of transubstantiation, the change of bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ. Other canons condemned heretics, set yearly provincial councils, barred new religious orders, and curbed clerical abuses. In the famous Canon 21, every Christian of age to confess and receive communion at least once a year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giraud-de-bor:
Giraud de Borneil was a Provençal troubadour born at Excideuil in the viscounty of Limoges around the middle of the twelfth century. His exact dates are unknown, but the best authorities place his life between 1160 and 1219. Of humble birth, he counted kings among his patrons, including Richard the Lionheart, whom he followed to Palestine on the Third Crusade. A Catholic Encyclopedia article calls him the master of the troubadours.

In winter he studied literature in the schools, and in summer, with two singers reciting his songs, he toured the courts of his royal patrons. Unmarried, he left his property at death to poor relations and his parish church of Saint-Gervais. About eighty poems survive with some certainty, scattered through collections. His early verse in the obscure trobar clus gave way to the easy, simple poetry he praised in his tensons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guayaquil:
Ecuador's port of Guayaquil, on the lower Guayas river, was founded by Benalcázar in 1535 and grew into the country's second city after Quito. Fear of earthquakes made it a city built almost wholly of wood, even its double-towered cathedral, so fire destroyed it again and again, most recently in 1896 and 1902.

Its bishopric, set up in February 1837 from Cuenca, first answered to Lima and then to Quito from 1849. It covers 11,500 square miles with 130,900 souls, 40 parishes, and a seminary and colleges. Bishops Garaycoa, Aguirre, and the Jesuits Lizarzabaru and del Pozo lead a roll that runs beside shipping figures, a Salesian school of 600 scholars, and a Dominican convent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-humeral-veil:
The humeral veil is a rectangular cloth about eight feet long and one and a half feet wide. It is worn over the back and shoulders, hence its name, with its ends hanging down in front. The Roman Ceremonial requires silk, edges are usually fringed, and a cross with the name Jesus or some other device adorns the centre. Festival veils are often richly embroidered.

Pockets or flaps under the lower edges let the wearer hold objects without wearing the veil itself out too fast. Clasps or ribbons across the breast keep it from slipping. The veil serves at solemn high Mass, where the subdeacon holds the paten in it from the Offertory to after the Pater Noster. It serves at pontifical Mass for the bishop's mitre, and in processions and benedictions where the sacred vessel must be carried veiled.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hyacinthe-sig:
Hyacinthe-Sigismond Gerdil was a Savoyard cardinal and theologian, born at Samoëns in 1718 and dead at Rome in 1802. At fifteen he joined the Barnabites at Annecy and studied theology at Bologna, where Archbishop Lambertini, later Benedict XIV, noticed his success across many branches of knowledge. He taught philosophy at Macerata and at Turin, became provincial of his order, and tutored the Prince of Piedmont.

Named cardinal in petto in 1773 by Clement XIV, Gerdil was promoted by Pius VI in 1777. Pius named him Dibbon's bishop, Holy Office consultor, corrector of oriental books, and Propaganda prefect. After Rome's invasion in 1798 he retired to his Abbey of Della Chiusa. At Venice in 1800 he would probably have been elected pope had Cardinal Herzan not vetoed him for the German emperor, and he then accompanied Pius VII to Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-de-montm:
John de Montmirail was a French nobleman who gave up court life and wealth for Cistercian poverty. Born in 1165 to the Lord of Montmirail, His mother trained him in piety. He embraced a military career and formed a lasting friendship with Philip Augustus at the royal court. Court dissipations dulled his early training, and even marriage to the estimable Helvide de Dampierre did not reform him.

In his thirtieth year the counsel of Jobert, prior of St. Etienne, converted him. He turned to God with generosity, building a hospital for the sick with special care for lepers. He loved the poor as brothers, wore a hair shirt, and spent whole nights in prayer. After trying the life of a recluse, he entered the Cistercian monastery of Longpont, giving his goods to the poor. He died in 1217, with miracles reported at his tomb ever since.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-kreil:
Karl Kreil was an Austrian meteorologist and astronomer, born at Ried in Upper Austria in 1798 and dead at Vienna in 1862. Schooled at Kremsmünster Abbey under Boniface Schwarzenbrunner, he joined its observatory work. He studied law for financial reasons, but abandoned it in 1823 for mathematics and physics. He served at Vienna in 1827, at Milan's Brera in 1831, and as director of Prague's observatory from 1845.

Finding Prague's observatory in poor condition, he turned to terrestrial observation and introduced terrestrial physics into Austria. Through personal privation he built a system of magnetic and meteorological observation rivaling Göttingen under Gauss. His plan for a central Austrian station was realized at Vienna in 1851, with Kreil as first director and professor of physics. His observations spread from Bohemia over the empire to the Adriatic, Turkey, and the Black Sea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liturgy-of-st:
The Liturgy of St. Basil gathers the Eastern rites linked to Basil, Bishop of Caesarea from 370 to 379. That Basil reshaped an older liturgy is firm, backed by Byzantine tradition and by many old witnesses, though several distinct forms now bear his name.

Proclus reports that Basil cut a long rite short when worshippers flagged, and Peter the Deacon quoted a Basil prayer in a letter around 520. Leontius praised Basil's rite against Theodore's new Mass, and the Trullan Council of 692 cited his written liturgy. The entry sorts the surviving Greek, Syriac, and other forms that claim his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-pierre-:
Louis Pierre Anquetil was a French historian, born at Paris in 1723 and dead in 1806. He joined the Congregation of Sainte-Geneviève at seventeen, taught theology and letters, directed the Reims seminary, and wrote a history of that city.

Prior at La Roee, director at Senlis, and holder of a priory at Chateau-Renard, he wrote a history of the League, then of the Fronde troubles. Jailed at Saint Lazare during the Terror, he worked there on his Universal History, finished after Thermidor. His History of France, done at Napoleon's request, shows old age's weakening grip, and Thierry judged it cold and colourless beside Mezeray and Daniel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-montreuil:
Montreuil is the Charterhouse of Notre-Dame-des-Pres in the Diocese of Arras, Pas-de-Calais. Its founder was Robert, Count of Boulogne and Auvergne. The charter bears the date 15 July 1324 from Hardelot castle, and the church was consecrated in 1338. Lying near Calais, it suffered repeated sackings by the English in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. At times it was abandoned.

Imperial troops wrecked it again in 1542. The wars of religion brought fresh troubles. Dom Bernard Bruyant rebuilt it late in the seventeenth century, leaving it quiet until the Revolution suppressed it in 1790 and sold its property. Eighty-two years later the Carthusians bought back part of the estate. They laid a new foundation stone in 1872 and finished in three years, with twenty-four cells and a noted press for order publications.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-odo-of-glanfe:
Odo of Glanfeuil, ninth-century abbot and hagiographer, gave Saint Maurus a French legend that scholars still doubt. Entering Glanfeuil by 856 and abbot by 861, he issued a Life of Maurus in 864, claiming to revise a life by Faustus of Montecassino that makes Maurus founder of Glanfeuil.

Its anachronisms persuade most critics that Odo wrote it himself, though Mabillon defended Faustus. Odo's Miracles of Saint Maurus, with more solid history, tells how he fled Normans with the relics in 862 and moved them to Saint-Maur-des-Fossés in 868. Mabillon and a few modern writers still ascribe the Life to Faustus, against the majority view.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paulus-bril:
Paulus Bril was a gifted Flemish painter and engraver born at Antwerp in 1556 and dead at Rome on 7 October 1626. He first studied with Damiaen Oertelmans. News of his brother Matthys's success at Rome drew him from his parents to that city. Held at Lyons for lack of funds, he worked to fund the journey onward.

At Rome he studied with his brother, but drew best inspiration later from copying Titian's landscapes. On that basis he built a vigorous style, said to have greatly advanced landscape art through influence on Rubens, Carracci, and Claude Lorraine. He aided his brother's Vatican works, and on Matthys's death in 1584 continued their joint labour for Gregory XIII. His chief Vatican work is a sixty-eight-foot fresco for the Sala Clementina, ordered by Clement VIII, showing Saint Clement cast into the sea with an anchor at his neck.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philippe-avri:
Philippe Avril was a French Jesuit traveller, born at Angoulême in 1654. Professor of philosophy and mathematics at Paris, he was summoned to the China missions and, following Father Verbiest's instructions from Peking, attempted the overland route. Six years of travel carried him through Kurdistan, Armenia, Astrakhan, Persia, and other eastern lands.

At Moscow he was refused passage through Tatary and sent by the government to Poland, from which he made his way to Constantinople and back to France. Worn out by haemorrhages, he nevertheless embarked again on a vessel that was lost at sea, and he died in the shipwreck of 1698. His accounts of his long wanderings remain interesting and valuable records of lands then little known to Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-plenary-counc:
A plenary council is a church synod that represents the whole body of bishops of a given territory. The Latin plenarium means complete or full, and Saint Augustine already called ecumenical councils plenary, since they represent the entire Church. Provincial councils earned the name because every bishop of the province attended.

Later usage narrowed the term to councils called by a delegate of the Apostolic See with special powers. Those councils were attended by all metropolitans and bishops of a kingdom or commonwealth or their representatives. Such synods are often called national councils, and the entry traces them from third-century gatherings at Iconium and Synnada through the plenary councils of all Africa under the Archbishop of Carthage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-polydore-verg:
Polydore Vergil was an Italian-born historian of England and a pioneer of modern historical method. He was born at Urbino about 1470, studied at Bologna and Padua, and served the Duke of Urbino and Alexander VI. His early works, a book of proverbs and On the Inventors of Things, won extraordinary popularity.

Sent to England in 1501 as sub-collector of Peter's Pence, he became intimate with Henry VII, who in 1505 commissioned his History of England. Published in 1533 and prized above all for Henry VII's reign, it consulted authorities, weighed evidence, and told a connected story rather than a bare chronicle. Offending Wolsey cost him prison and his collectorship, and he avenged himself with a hostile portrait of Wolsey in the history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-provincial-co:
A provincial council is a deliberative assembly of the bishops of a church province. The metropolitan archbishop calls it and chairs it, to debate common business and set disciplinary rules. This encyclopedia entry shows why such groupings arose. A church as vast as the Catholic Church needed dioceses with shared interests to act together while general canon law was still taking shape. Early councils ordered bishops to meet twice a year, at Nicaea in 325 and Antioch in 341.

Attendance was a strict duty for bishops. Those who stayed away without good excuse faced censure. In early times slack bishops lost communion with their fellows. Others joined for counsel without a vote. They included non-exempt abbots, deputies of cathedral chapters, heads of religious orders, university deputies, seminary rectors, and the council's theologians and canonists. The entry closes by pointing to the great collections where decrees from Trent to 1870 are printed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-vei:
In ancient Rome a red veil, or one with red stripes, marked newly married women apart from the unmarried. From the earliest times Christ was set before the Christian virgin as a husband, the only one, in Saint Paul's words, she had to please. As the vestal virgins had done, the bride of Christ naturally took the veil, which symbolized less purity than inviolable fidelity to Christ, a fidelity to be reverenced in her. Saint Optatus called the bond a sort of spiritual marriage.

Taking the veil thus suggested an obligation of constancy: first it forbade illicit intercourse, and afterwards marriage itself. Virgins took the veil themselves or received it from their parents' hands. Widows who professed continence wore it too, and the entry follows the veil from Roman marriage custom into the consecration of virgins in the Roman Pontifical.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rene-goupil:
René Goupil, Jesuit missionary, was born in Anjou in 1607 and martyred in New York State on 23 September 1642. Poor health kept him from joining the Society regularly, so he volunteered to serve it without pay in Canada as a donné. After two years as a surgeon in the Quebec hospitals, he set out in 1642 for the Huron mission with Father Jogues, remaining his constant companion and disciple until death.

Captured by the Iroquois near Lake Saint Peter, he accepted his fate without resistance. He shared the other captives' beating: nails torn out, finger joints cut off. The thirteen days' march to Iroquois country brought heat, hunger, blows, and festering wounds. Forced to march between double ranks of two hundred warriors, he was almost beaten to death, yet when he might have escaped, he stayed with Jogues.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-lalor:
Richard Lalor Sheil was an Irish dramatist, writer, and politician whose voice helped carry the campaign for Catholic Emancipation. Born in County Kilkenny in 1791, he was schooled at home, at Kensington, and at Stonyhurst, then entered Trinity College Dublin and qualified at the Irish Bar in 1814. When family money failed, he turned to the stage, and plays such as Adelaide, The Apostate, and Evadne brought him both fame and income.

Politics soon claimed more of his energy. At first he favoured gentle petitioning and compromise with Protestant opinion, but he came round to Daniel O'Connell's bolder agitation, demanding emancipation as a right rather than a favour. In the Catholic Association he stood second only to O'Connell, and his Sketches of the Irish Bar preserved vivid portraits of the lawyers and leaders of his day. He died at Florence in 1851.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-nanteu:
Robert Nanteuil was a French engraver and crayon portraitist who raised engraving to fine art. Born at Reims in 1623, a merchant's son, he was sent to a Jesuit school that gave him learning but no encouragement to draw. In spare moments he worked with pencil and burin. Benedictines later fostered his gift; one monk sat for his Buste d'un Religieux of 1644.

In financial straits, he went to Paris in 1648 and worked with Regnesson, whose sister he married. His method moved from straight lines alone to cross-hatching and stippling for middle tones. Crayon portraits won him a pension and the post of Royal Engraver in 1658, with a Gobelins studio. In 1660 Louis XIV, largely at his prompting, issued an edict giving engravers the privileges of other artists. He made nineteen portraits of the king alone and wrote verses often printed beneath his portraits. He died at Paris in 1678.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rule-of-st-ba:
Under the name Basilians fall all religious who follow the Rule of St Basil. Their monasteries never had the organization of a proper order's houses. Basil drew up his Rule for the monastery he founded about 356 on the Iris in Cappadocia, after visiting Egypt, Palestine, and Mesopotamia. Gregory of Nazianzus, who shared the retreat, aided him with advice and experience.

The Rule divides into Greater Monastic Rules and Lesser Rules. Rufinus, translating them into Latin, joined both into a single Rule followed by some western monasteries. Basil's method is catechetical: the disciple poses a question, the master answers. He lays down indisputable principles to guide superiors and monks, sending them to Scripture as the true Rule. Questions concern virtues to practise and vices to avoid. Its striking qualities are prudence and wisdom: superiors settle daily details, while poverty, obedience, renunciation, and self-abnegation ground monastic life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-santa-maria-b:
Santa Maria, a Brazilian see suffragan of Porto Alegre, was one of three new sees cut from São Pedro do Rio Grande do Sul. Pius X raised that see to an archdiocese on 15 August 1910. Pelotas and Uruguayana were the other two. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia sketches a young diocese of farming colonies.

Santa Maria holds twenty-two parishes across the central and northern parts of Rio Grande do Sul, a mild, wooded, fertile country where German and Italian colonists farm and raise cattle. Nearly everyone is Catholic. Cachoeira on the Jacuhy river, 120 miles west of Porto Alegre by steamboat and rail, ranks as chief town, with Rio Pardo, Santa Maria, Passo Fundo, and Cruz Alta behind it. Lima de Valverde became first bishop in 1911.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sao-paulo-bra:
São Paulo, an ecclesiastical province in Brazil, gathers the dioceses of Campinas, Ribeirão Preto, Taubaté, Botucatú, Corityba, and São Carlos do Pinhal, all in São Paulo state. Made a bishopric in 1745, it rose to metropolitan rank in 1908, when those dioceses were created with it. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia gives the province's strength in figures.

Over 2,500,000 Catholics lived in the province in 1910, served by 203 secular and fifty regular priests across seven orders, with four convents, 530 churches and chapels, and thirty-six Catholic schools. In the city of São Paulo stand the provincial and central seminaries and a girls' seminary under the Sisters of St Joseph. Benedictine and Marist colleges and the Lyceu of Our Lady of Mount Carmel complete the list.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-second-latera:
The Second Lateran Council, tenth ecumenical council, was convoked by Innocent II in April 1139 after a schism that followed Honorius II's death in February 1130. Petrus Leonis, as Anacletus II, long checked the lawful pope, backed by Bernard and Norbert, until Anacletus died in January 1138. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a council meant to erase a schism's traces.

Innocent had held a council at Pisa in 1135 and gained ground steadily. At the Lateran nearly a thousand prelates from most Christian nations gathered. The pope opened with a discourse and deposed those ordained or instituted by the antipope and his chief backers, Aegidius of Tusculum and Gerard of Angoulême. Roger of Sicily, Anacletus's partisan reconciled with Innocent, still upheld schism in southern Italy, and the council condemned errors and reformed clerical and popular abuses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-boisil:
St. Boisil was superior of Melrose Abbey, dead in 664, and this entry follows a man known almost entirely from Bede. Almost all we know of Boisil comes from Bede's Ecclesiastical History and Life of Cuthbert. Bede learned it from Sigfrid, a monk of Jarrow previously trained by Boisil at Melrose. Boisil's fame rests mainly on his great pupil, St. Cuthbert, but the master was plainly worthy of the disciple.

Boisil's supernatural intuitions deeply impressed his contemporaries. When Cuthbert arrived at Melrose, Boisil exclaimed, Behold a servant of the Lord, and got Abbot Eata's leave to receive him into the community at once. When Cuthbert fell sick in the great pestilence of 664, Boisil declared his certain recovery. Somewhat later Boisil himself, as foretold three years before, fell victim to that epidemic, but before the end he predicted Cuthbert would become a bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-holy-grai:
A legendary sacred vessel, sometimes the chalice of the Eucharist and sometimes the dish of the Paschal lamb, anchors this entry on medieval romance. In the romances its nature shifts and often stays vague; Chrétien's Perceval leaves it wholly unexplained. Its name too has drawn many guesses, and the entry sifts them with care.

Helinandus, a Cistercian chronicler who died about 1230, supplies the accepted account. Under the year 717 he tells of a hermit's vision of the dish used at the Last Supper, written up as the Gradale. French gradalis meant a wide, deep dish serving costly foods in courses, while popular speech called it greal, pleasant to the eater. Romance cycles built a quest upon it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-third-lateran:
Lateran Council of 1179, third of that name, closes this slice with Alexander III's laborious pontificate. Like 1139, its task was to repair evils from an antipope's schism. Back in Rome on 12 March 1178, Alexander took citizens' oaths of fidelity and needful guarantees. He then welcomed antipope Callistus III, John de Struma, who yielded at Tusculum on 29 August 1178 after Christian of Mainz besieged him at Viterbo.

Alexander received Callistus with kindness and made him Governor of Beneventum. Obstinate partisans picked Lando Sitino as a new antipope Innocent III, but lacking support he soon gave up and retired to La Cava monastery. In September 1178, under the Peace of Venice, the pope called an ecumenical council at the Lateran for the next Lent, sending legates far and wide. Its canons on elections and discipline shaped the medieval Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vatican-counc:
The Vatican Council, the twentieth ecumenical council and, to 1912, the last, opened on 8 December 1869 and adjourned on 20 October 1870, three hundred years after Trent. Its earlier history begins on 6 December 1864, two days before the Syllabus appeared, when Pius IX told the Congregation of Rites of his plan to summon a general council. He asked Rome's cardinals to write their views on the plan's wisdom and on subjects for discussion.

Of twenty-one reports sent in, only Cardinal Pentini's held that no council was needed; the rest backed the scheme. The entry follows the preparations, the council's sessions, its debates on faith and on papal infallibility, and its abrupt adjournment when Italian troops entered Rome. It closes with the council's constitutions and their reception, a full history of a council cut short by war.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vaudreuil:
Philippe de Rigaud, Marquis de Vaudreuil, governed Canada as its governor, born in Languedoc in the first half of the seventeenth century to Louis de Vaudreuil and Marie de Château-Verdun. He died at Quebec on 10 October 1725. In the king's musketeers, where he served from 1659 to 1676, he rose to brigadier and finally colonel. He reached Canada in 1687 commanding a marine detachment.

After the Lachine massacre he kept the Iroquois from attacking Montreal in 1689, and in 1690 he shared in Quebec's defence against Phips. In 1698 he won the Cross of St Louis and succeeded Callières as Governor of Montreal. In 1702 he received the fief still bearing his name, and in 1703 he again succeeded Callières, now as governor-general, guiding the colony through a trying age.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BurglassCecil_B: Harold Weisberg, by the evidence of his files, wrote this memo on a meeting with Cecil Burglass concerning the Ray case, the prosecution of James Earl Ray for the King assassination. govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FerrieDavidWill:
Southern Research Company, a private investigation firm, prepared a background synopsis on David William Ferrie. The report lays out who Ferrie was on paper. It includes his arrests in Jefferson Parish on morals charges, among them carnal knowledge and contributing to the delinquency of a juvenile.

Ferrie later drew the attention of investigators looking into the Kennedy assassination in New Orleans. A background report of this kind is what investigators build first: addresses, arrests, and reputation in one digest. This one preserves the firm's findings on a man whose name would not stay private for long.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GouldstonPhil_G: Harold Weisberg wrote on March 9, 1973 to a man named Jim, whose surname is illegible, about the commercial representation of assassination books. govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_colombia: Former Colombian president Álvaro Uribe was known by the nickname El Viejo, the old man. This briefing-book page presents declassified records said to detail suspected paramilitary and drug ties among his circle. The evidence supplied here is the title alone, and the underlying records are not described. Because the claims are allegations in documents rather than court findings, the page is best used as a guide to records that readers must weigh for themselves.
in-times-of-peril: In Times of Peril, G. A. Henty's Indian Mutiny tale. The perilous times. This book preserves that historical novel. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
isobel-a-romance-of-the-northern-trail:
James Oliver Curwood's Isobel is a romance of the northern trail, set a thousand miles north of civilisation at Point Fullerton. It opens with Sergeant William MacVeigh of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police. He reports his hunt for Scottie Deane, a murderer, across three hundred miles of Hudson Bay shore and sixteen hundred miles of patrol country.

Curwood builds his story from Mounted Police patrols and Barren Lands travel. The harsh beauty of the far north presses hard on his characters, where law, love and survival contend. Isobel herself enters as the woman at the heart of the romance, and the trail romance of the title binds pursuit and passion together. Readers who like adventure stories of the Canadian north, written by one of its most popular early novelists, will find Isobel swift and atmospheric.
nasa-tm-19710069673-photographic-study-o:
E William Conrad, Ned P Hannum, and Harry E Bloomer of the Lewis Research Center filmed boiling inside a rocket engine injector. Their subject was the RL-10 engine during throttled, low power running. At such settings the engine could chug, a rough pulsing combustion fault. High speed motion pictures looked into the liquid oxygen cavity of the injector. A film supplement accompanied the report.

The catalog record explains what the cameras watched. Liquid oxygen boiled inside the cavity while the engine ran in the chugging range. Crew injected helium gas to steady the burning. The films showed conditions as that gas entered. Watching the fault directly helped engineers understand chugging. It also showed whether the helium cure truly worked.
openings-in-the-old-trail:
Bret Harte, the best-known storyteller of the California gold country, gathered nine tales in Openings in the Old Trail. The titles alone sketch his territory: a foothills messenger, Colonel Starbottle pleading a case, and a hotel landlord at the Big Flume. There is also an inheritance in Buckeye Hollow, and a figure called the Goddess of Excelsior.

The opening story plants a boy, Leonidas Boone, under a dwarf fir at burning noon on Casket Ridge. He refuses to move until the tree's shadow creeps to a chosen stone, for no reason he could give. Harte tells the small ordeal with dry humor and close observation. That mixture of local color, sentiment, and irony made his western tales famous on two continents.
pee-wee-harris-on-the-trail: The sample provided here shows only the front matter of Pee-wee Harris on the Trail, the title page and contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names Percy Keese Fitzhugh and illustrator H. S. Barbour, and notes the approval of the Boy Scouts of America. The contents promise a lone figure, three good turns, robbers, a message in the dark, a race with death, and camp scenes, the mixture of the Pee-wee Harris scout stories.
report-of-the-special-committee-on-moral:
New Zealand's Special Committee on Moral Delinquency in Children and Adolescents sent this report to the Prime Minister on September 20, 1954. R. E. Owen, Government Printer at Wellington, printed it that year. The matter had been referred to the committee on July 23, 1954, and its members agreed on the report and its counsel.

O. C. Mazengarb chaired the committee, with R. A. Bloodworth, J. Leggat, G. L. McLeod, Lucy V. O'Brien, J. S. Somerville, and F. N. Stace as members. Four volumes of witness evidence went with the report, plus a large file of written submissions. The report was laid upon the table of the House of Representatives.
sammie-and-susie-littletail: Howard R. Garis wrote Sammie and Susie Littletail, with pictures by Louis Wisa, dated 1910. The contents list thirty-one chapters, opening with Sammie Littletail in a Trap, Sammie Littletail Is Rescued, and What Happened to Susie Littletail. Later chapters cover Papa Littletail's picture, a new burrow, help for Mrs. Wren, and Uncle Wiggily getting shot.
shallow-soil:
Knut Hamsun wrote this novel, here in an approved English version by Carl Christian Hyllested. The translator's preface tells how Hamsun burst on Europe in the autumn of 1888, when chapters of a life-based novel ran in a Danish magazine. Ibsen, Bjornson, and Strindberg then ruled northern letters, yet Hamsun's name was new.

Hyllested traces the long, bitter struggle behind that sudden blaze of fame. Want and defeat had strewn Hamsun's path for years. The novel itself turns to young city lives and thin hopes, drawn by a writer who knew shallow ground by hard personal trial.
sons-of-the-soil:
Honoré de Balzac gives Sons of the Soil to Monsieur P. S. B. Gavault. Katharine Prescott Wormeley turned the book into English. A long dedication opens the volume. Balzac borrows words from Rousseau for its head. I have seen the morals of my time, they run. For his part, Balzac has studied his epoch's march. He publishes this work as a study of it.

His aim is to show a class long passed over. That class is the peasants of France. Writers make criminals poetic, Balzac charges. They all but deify the town working man. None has dared face the country wilds, he says. There a plot runs without cease. Peasant stands against landowner in that plot. The peasant gnaws the soil into a hundred scraps.
the-blazed-trail:
Stewart Edward White dedicated his logging novel to his father, from whose early pioneer life many of Harry Thorpe's experiences were drawn. Contents divide the book into the forest, the landlooker, the blazing of the trail, Thorpe's dream girl, and the following of the trail.

Part one opens with a portrait of the American pioneer as picturesque, resourceful, self-reliant, and bold. Such a man adapts fast, learns from beasts and neighbours, and meets danger with cheerful confidence. He needs little from towns, substituting rawhide for leather and venison for canned goods. White presents woods life as elemental, with epic dramas and a clear eye that marks the advance guard.
the-boy-aviators-in-africa-or-an-aerial-:
Captain Wilbur Lawton wrote The Boy Aviators in Africa, or An Aerial Ivory Trail. Its chapters run from a reunion and stolen ivory to the dark continent and a witch-doctor. The Pool of Death, a traitor in camp, and a battle in the air come next. Slave-traders, gorillas, and a rogue elephant crowd the late chapters.

The first chapter opens in a rush of packs and talk. Harry is told to catch hold, then yelps that a cartridge box fell on his sore corn. A third voice asks if the crew is bound for Africa or on a Coney Island picnic. Billy Barnes, a reporter, is told to be grave now. The talk is brisk and comic, and it sets the crew in motion.
the-cauldron-of-oil:
Wilkie Collins wrote this crime tale, dated 1861 in its heading. The scene is Croix-Daurade, a village about a league from Toulouse in France. Collins notes that the place is known in English military history for a charge of the eighteenth hussars, and in French criminal history for a bold crime.

The story opens in the year 1700 with the cast named one by one. First comes the village priest, Pierre-Celestin Chaubard, a plain, sociable man held in high regard by his flock. Then comes the Siadoux family, headed by Saturnin Siadoux, a widowed oil maker of sixty with five children. Collins presents the case as a plain narrative of a crime found out and punished under strange facts.
the-choise-of-valentines-or-the-merie-ba:
Thomas Nash's bawdy poem, The Choise of Valentines, also called the merie ballad of Nash his dildo, survives only in manuscript copies. John S. Farmer edited it for a private printing for subscribers only, dated 1899 in Roman numerals. The copies used sit in the Inner Temple library, dated about 1680, and in the Bodleian, dated about 1610 to 1620.

Farmer's introduction is candid about the poem's worth. It is doubtful, he says, that the piece was ever printed before, and by merit alone it would not earn print now. Its claim is different: the world cannot afford to lose any document that may bear on knowledge of the past. The edition thus keeps a frank, comic Elizabethan poem in reach of scholars. Line notes, moved to the end of each poem, help readers follow the text without breaking its flow.
the-danger-trail:
James Oliver Curwood's The Danger Trail, dated 1910, lays out seventeen chapters in its contents. They run from The Girl of the Snows and The Mysterious Attack through The House of the Red Death and Jean's Story. A final chapter is named Meleese. Chapter I, The Girl of the Snows, opens on Howland under a polar sky.

For perhaps the first time in his life, Howland feels romance, adventure, and love of the picturesque surge through him. A billion stars glow like yellow, passionless eyes. Behind him the icy Saskatchewan twists white through snow-smothered wilds, with a few lights where Prince Albert, the last outpost of settled life, comes down to the river half a mile away. He looks north into white gloom reaching a thousand miles to the Arctic Sea.
the-daredevil: Maria Thompson Daviess, author of The Melting of Molly and Miss Selina Lue, published The Daredevil in 1916, with a frontispiece painted by E. Sophonisba Hergesheimer and a dedication to Jessie Morson Grahame. Its contents list fifteen chapters with titles such as Sparkling Waves over High Explosives, Vive la France!, That Mr. G. Slade of Detroit, The Impossible Uncle Robert, and Behold, I Am a Spy! Only the front matter and contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear.
the-emigrant-trail: Geraldine Bonner's The Emigrant Trail, copyrighted in 1910, is present here as title matter and a bare list of parts. The parts are named The Prairie, The River, The Mountains, and The Desert. A fifth part is left unnamed in the list. A frontispiece shows a man bearing a woman back into a dark cavern. No story text appears in these pages.
the-enchanted-april:
Elizabeth von Arnim's The Enchanted April opens in a London women's club on a grey February day. Mrs. Wilkins, down from Hampstead to shop, scans The Times in the smoking room. She stops at a small ad. A furnished medieval Italian castle stands on the Mediterranean. It is to let for April. The ad speaks to those who prize wistaria and sunshine. The thought takes root before she knows it.

Four unlike women share the castle to escape damp lives and dull marriages. Sun, sea, and rest work slow change on each. Von Arnim's tale is light on its feet and warm at heart.
the-first-of-april: An unsigned poem called The First of April, or The Triumphs of Folly is present here only in its front matter. The title page was printed at London in 1777. It gives the work to the author of The Diaboliad. It quotes Shakespeare on the name of fool. It names the price of two shillings and sixpence. A dedication to a famed duchess begins at the end. No verse of the poem itself is included in this portion.
the-great-salt-lake-trail:
Colonel Henry Inman and Colonel William F. Cody wrote The Great Salt Lake Trail. Inman was a late assistant quartermaster in the United States Army. Cody, called Buffalo Bill, was a late chief of scouts. The book's first edition is dated 1898. Its preface surveys the seven historic trails of the plains. All of them cross what is now Kansas. None but the old Santa Fe trail, the preface says, has a more stirring story than the Salt Lake Trail.

Over that highway the Mormons made their lonely Hegira to the valley of the great inland sea. On its shores they founded a city. The preface calls it marvellous in conception, a monument to man's power over hard odds. The same route carried the expeditions of Fremont, Stansbury, and Lander. Over it the Pony Express made its feats of speed.
the-iron-trail: Rex Beach wrote this Alaskan railroad novel. His earlier books include The Spoilers. Only the title page and contents are present here. The story itself does not appear. The headings move in his brisk style. The tide takes a hand first. A girl appears out of the night. An Irish prince and a journey to Hope follow. Curtis Gordon shows his teeth, then fails in his cunning. The battle of Gordon's crossing comes midway. A prince becomes a man, then a prince again.
the-ivory-trail:
Talbot Mundy opens this tale in Edward Monty. Its first part is the story of the yerkes. Monty is an elderly English country gentleman. His hobby is fox hunting. His stud runs to four thoroughbreds. The Marquis of Montbar himself keeps him company. Social eminence follows him out hunting. A man of sterling worth is how he is rated. He answers his letters in faultless copperplate.

His horses change at every town and village. He keeps decent company if England offers any. His peers respect him; his park impresses everyone. His secret lies in a hard education. Trials and experience taught him method. The tale will carry that method into Africa. The ivory will test it. Mundy builds an English facade first, then takes it abroad.
the-jubilee-of-the-constitution-delivere:
John Quincy Adams delivered this oration in New York on April 30, 1839. The New York Historical Society heard it. Fifty years had passed since Washington took the presidential oath. Adams opens with a licensed flight of fancy. On the night before that first swearing-in, an angel appears. The angel wears Washington's mother's form. He brings a suit of heavenly armor for the Father of his Country.

Each piece of the armor is named. The helmet is piety, justice, honor, and kindness. The spear is studded with the Declaration's self-evident truths. The sword is the one Washington led armies with. The shield is the Constitution itself. Heavenly hands embossed it with the people's future history. Adams then turns to the thirteen colonies' settlers. English, Dutch, Swedish, German, and French stock mixed in them.
the-last-trail:
Zane Grey published his frontier novel in 1909. Twilight falls over the wild Ohio valley as a traveler nears the end of a rough journey toward Fort Henry. His guide quit that morning with a thin excuse, and his teamster knows nothing of the frontier.

Mr. Sheppard warns the men to speak low so his daughter will not hear their fear. His son Will admits the guide acted like a man expecting trouble or fearing an attack. Grey builds danger from darkness, a lonely trail, and a party that suspects betrayal too late to turn back.
the-lifted-veil:
No author is named on the opening pages of this tale, which begin with a verse motto and a dying narrator. He suffers attacks of angina pectoris, and his physician gives him only months to live. A stranger curse matters more to him than the illness.

He claims foresight of his own death down to its date, September 20, 1850, at ten at night in his study. He can also foresee every event of his last moments, since insight and foresight have wearied his whole life. A tale of second sight, a femme fatale, and dread unfolds from that confession.
the-little-regiment-and-other-episodes-o:
Stephen Crane's The Little Regiment gathers six episodes of the American Civil War: the title story, Three Miraculous Soldiers, A Mystery of Heroism, An Indiana Campaign, A Grey Sleeve, and The Veteran. The title story opens in thick fog, where an infantry column in a roadway looks like a long, low shadow in the mist. Above the ranks hovers a muttering that is one part grumble and three parts joke.

Across a little river, a battered town looms through grey cloud, its belfry still pointing at the sky after bombardment. Guns on distant heights thunder while hidden masses of men and artillery shake the earth. Crane writes war as weather, noise, and confusion, with ordinary soldiers moving through a landscape they can barely see.
the-long-labrador-trail: Dillon Wallace, author of The Lure of the Labrador Wild, wrote The Long Labrador Trail, dated 1917 and dedicated to his wife's memory. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the narrative itself does not appear. The nineteen chapters trace an expedition. Titles include The Voice of the Wilderness, On the Old Indian Trail, We Go Astray, and Seal Lake at Last. Disaster in the Rapids, Caught by the Arctic Ice, and To Whale River and Fort Chimo follow. Closing chapters treat Labrador's Indians and Eskimos.
the-lost-trail:
Edward S. Ellis wrote The Lost Trail, a frontier tale in thirty-three chapters. Chapter one, An Enemy in a Tree, opens on an early-spring afternoon. A sturdy youth of seventeen, Jack Carleton, follows a clearly marked trail through the western part of Kentucky toward the Mississippi River. The contents widen the setting: chapters on the bank of the Mississippi, a visitor from the other shore, the Louisiana shore, a primitive fort, and an aboriginal home.

A recurring figure in the chapter titles is Deerfoot, whose maneuvers get a chapter of their own. Titles like At Bay, The Eavesdropper, Within the Wigwam, and Pursuer and Pursued promise chases and reversals. Ellis writes the kind of frontier adventure in which a boy, a trail, and a skilled Native scout carry the action.
the-patrol-of-the-sun-dance-trail:
Ralph Connor wrote The Patrol of the Sun Dance Trail. The contents list twenty-one chapters, from The Trail-Runner to Why the Doctor Stayed. Chapter One opens high on a hillside among jack pines in Kicking Horse Pass, where the Union Jack marks the headquarters of Superintendent Strong of the North West Mounted Police.

Strong's duty is to keep law and order along the Canadian Pacific Railway construction line. Below, a dark, wiry man comes running up the tote road, panting and streaming with exhaustion. He turns up a side trail toward the flag and struggles to the wooden shack. Connor opens a western tale of police, railway builders, and the peoples of the passes.
the-pupil:
Henry James wrote the novella presented here in the Le Roy Phillips edition published at Boston in 1916, following the Definitive Edition text. A young tutor named Pemberton arrives to discuss taking charge of an eleven-year-old boy in the Moreen household.

The opening chapter stays on an awkward negotiation. Mrs. Moreen talks warmly about feelings while avoiding any mention of pay, and Pemberton hesitates to raise money at all. The boy Morgan is sent out for a fan and returns without it, already showing the sharp, difficult character the tutor will have to handle.
the-rainbow-trail: Zane Grey calls his romance a sequel in spirit, opening with a foreword and chapters set at Red Lake, a sagi, Kayenta, and a hidden valley. Headings follow a trail through hogans, desert trials, a place called Surprise Valley, Navajo episodes, wild justice, and a final approach to Nonnezoshe at the foot of the rainbow. Only the title pages and contents list are present here, so the desert narrative itself does not appear.
the-u-p-trail:
Zane Grey frames his western novel with a long passage from Robert Louis Stevenson praising the railway age. Stevenson calls the line pushed through an unwatered wilderness an epic subject, mixing gold, violence, makeshift towns, and frock-coated gentlemen behind the work. Grey then begins his own story in the early eighteen-sixties.

Chapter one follows the old trail westward from the broad Missouri across Nebraska's grassy plains toward Wyoming. Buffalo herds, wolves, trappers' campfires, rocky gorges, and high passes fill the journey onward into Utah, Nevada, and California. The opening builds the land itself into a character before the human drama of the Union Pacific route unfolds.
the-white-devil:
No author's name is printed in the pages preserved here for the tragedy The White Devil. An address to the reader defends publishing the play at all. The production, the writer complains, was acted in a dull winter time. It played in an open, black theatre, lacking a full and understanding auditory. That audience, he says, is the only grace and setting-out of a tragedy.

Playgoers since resemble ignorant asses at stationers' shops, he adds, asking for new books rather than good ones. Accused of slowness in finishing, he answers with Euripides. The Greek composed three verses in three days, against another writer's three hundred. The other's verses would be read for three days, his own for three ages. He praises Chapman, Jonson, Beaumont, and Fletcher while expecting detraction, ignorance's sworn friend.
tom-slade-on-mystery-trail: Percy Keese Fitzhugh wrote Tom Slade on Mystery Trail, illustrated by R. Emmett Owen and published by Grosset and Dunlap at New York in 1921. The Boy Scouts of America approved the book. Fitzhugh also wrote the Roy Blakeley books and other Tom Slade titles. A contents heading begins at the end of what is present, but no chapter titles follow it. The title and copyright pages are what is held in this record, so Fitzhugh's story itself does not appear.
tom-swift-and-his-wizard-camera-or-thril: Thrilling Adventures While Taking Moving Pictures is the subtitle of the Tom Swift wizard camera story by Victor Appleton, presented through twenty-five chapter headings. A strange offer and a man in a snow bank open the book. Later headings travel to India for an elephant stampede and lion fight, then snap an avalanche, a native battle, a jungle fire, and a volcano's molten rim. An earthquake concludes the list. Chapter one is announced without text following. The contents list alone is shown in this record.
un-sc-res-colin-powell-s-february-5-2003:
Colin Powell, the United States secretary of state, addressed the Security Council on February 5, 2003, to make the case for war with Iraq. He spoke for more than an hour, using tapes, satellite photos, and a small vial held up for the cameras. Millions watched the session live.

Powell argued that Iraq hid weapons of mass destruction and mobile labs for germ warfare. He said Baghdad had failed its last chance to disarm. No such weapons were found after the invasion weeks later. The address is now studied as a famous failure of intelligence and persuasion.
un-sc-res-zulfiqar-ali-bhutto-s-farewell:
Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto, Pakistan's foreign minister, gave this farewell speech to the Security Council in December 1971. The Council had just voted on the war between India and Pakistan over East Pakistan, soon to become Bangladesh. Bhutto charged that the Council had failed his country at its hour of need.

He closes by tearing up his papers, declaring he would not be party to a shameful surrender, and walking out of the hall. The scene became one of the most famous in UN history. The speech itself is a fierce attack on great-power politics, in the speaker's own words.
vanguards-of-the-plains-a-romance-of-the: Margaret Hill McCarter, author of The Price of the Prairie, wrote Vanguards of the Plains, a romance of the old Santa Fe Trail, issued by Harper and Brothers in 1917. She dedicated it to the memory of the men who defied the desert, walked the prairies boldly, and died bravely while building a highway for a westward-moving empire. Pages present here hold front matter only: title pages, that dedication, and the start of a contents list whose first part is called Clearing the Trail. The story itself is not shown.
voyage-of-the-paper-canoe-a-geographical: An old Project Gutenberg header identifies this file as Voyage of the Paper Canoe by N. H. Bishop, released as etext number 1082 in October 1997. The pages present here are that header only, with its talk of volunteers, donations, and keeping the file whole for the next readers. No title page, contents, or lines of Bishop's journey down the American rivers in a paper canoe are shown. The header alone names the work, its author, and its place in the Gutenberg list.
vril: Edward Bulwer Lytton wrote Vril: The Power of the Coming Race, dated 1875 in the file header. Pages present here hold that header, the doubled title, and a bare list of chapter numbers running past twenty, so the novel itself is not shown. The list skips from chapter sixteen to chapter eighteen, a gap the pages do not explain. Nothing here names the underground race, their strange power called vril, or the traveler who finds them. Readers learn only the frame of Lytton's tale of a hidden world below the earth.
